articles.title: UK CBAM records: why net mass, not CMR weight, matters - Trans.INFO
articles.summary: UK CBAM records: why net mass, not CMR weight, matters  Trans.INFO
articles.full_text:
Key points:
- UK CBAM applies to imports of aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, and iron and steel from 1 January 2027.
- Importers of £50,000 or more of CBAM goods in 12 months will be liable.
- For each import, they must record net mass in kilograms, excluding packaging, to up to 6 decimal places.
- Forwarders, hauliers and customs brokers do not become the importer by acting on the importer’s behalf.
- Importers that do not keep records may face a £500 fixed penalty.
Who pays
UK CBAM puts a carbon price on imports of five sectors: aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, and iron and steel. The aim is for imported goods to face a carbon cost comparable to that paid by UK producers.
The tax is paid by the importer. According to HMRC, this is the person named on the import declaration, even if someone else declares the goods for them. HMRC lists freight forwarders, hauliers (drivers), customs brokers, express operators and fast parcel operators among those who may import goods on someone else’s behalf. In all these cases, the business it is acting for “will still be classed as the importer”.
A business is liable once its CBAM imports reach £50,000 in 12 months, or if it expects to reach that amount within the next 30 days, according to the registration rules.
Gross weight is not enough
This is where transport companies come in. Under HMRC’s record-keeping guidance, importers must keep the following for every CBAM import from 1 January 2027:
- the 8-digit commodity code and a description of the goods,
- net mass in kilograms, excluding packaging, to up to 6 decimal places,
- the value of the goods,
- the date the goods entered the UK or cleared customs,
- proof of origin and evidence of any exemptions.
The records must be kept for 6 years. HMRC lists import declarations, bills of lading, commercial invoices, packing lists and “carrier weight records” among the documents that can support them.
In practice, a CMR or delivery note usually shows gross weight, including pallets and packaging. To get the net figure, importers will need packing lists or data from manufacturers. HMRC notes that weight evidence “might be from manufacturers”.
No border stop, but more data requests
CBAM is not collected at the border. Importers will register from 1 January 2028 and submit their first return and payment by 31 May 2028, covering imports from 2027.
However, importers will need the data from the very first shipment in January. Those who cannot obtain verified actual emissions data must use default values, and failing to keep records may lead to a fixed penalty of £500.
For forwarders and hauliers handling steel, aluminium or fertiliser loads into the UK, this means more requests for accurate documents. Customers may ask for packing lists, net weights and weighbridge records with each consignment, so it pays to agree in advance who provides which data.
For more on the basics, see our guides on who pays UK CBAM and on the HMRC rulebook published earlier this month.

articles.title: Steel: Confimi’s Italian foundries take on Brussels – tariffs and the CBAM are hurting the supply chain - Eunews
articles.summary: Steel: Confimi’s Italian foundries take on Brussels – tariffs and the CBAM are hurting the supply chain  Eunews
articles.full_text:
Brussels – “Four months after the new European regime on steel imports came into force, almost 30 per cent of companies in the foundry and engineering sectors have seen a fall in orders due to rules that make it cheaper to buy semi-finished products from outside the EU.” This is how Flavio Lorenzin, president of Confimi Industria Meccanica, summarises in a statement the critical issues that emerged during the conference organised yesterday in Padua by the trade association together with Confimi Industria Veneto and Confimi Industria Padova-Rovigo. The companies present described difficulties that are jeopardising the continuity of production and fuelling mistrust towards the decisions taken in Brussels.
At the heart of the criticism lies an asymmetry in the trade defence system. “The EU imposes duties on imports of metallic materials when they enter as raw materials, but applies them at a negligible rate – or virtually none at all – when metal products are imported as semi-finished goods. The metal is the same; it is who pays that changes: companies that buy it as a raw material bear the cost, while those that import it in a processed form do not,” explains Lorenzin.
From 1 July 2026, the European regulation provides for a 50 per cent duty on steel imports exceeding the annual quotas, compared with 25 per cent under the previous safeguard measure. Furthermore, from 1 January, with the final phase of the CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism), imports of cast iron, steel, and aluminium will also be subject to a charge linked to carbon dioxide emissions. Melted metals and many processed components from third countries, however, remain exempt from both mechanisms: the Commission has proposed extending the CBAM to over 400 downstream products from 2028, but the text is still under negotiation.
Meanwhile, prices are soaring. “From November 2025 to the present day, costs have risen by an average of 13 per cent for carbon steels, 16 per cent for stainless steels and 37 per cent for aluminium,” the chairman explains.
“Defending ‘Made in Italy’ is a political choice: if production costs in Europe are not reduced, businesses will either close or relocate,” warns Lorenzin. “We need lower taxes, less bureaucracy, competitively priced energy, flexible regulations, and a reduced tax wedge. And the cost of imports must be brought into line with the costs borne by European businesses.”
The association is therefore calling on Brussels to review import duties and to include semi-finished products, castings, and components in the CBAM negotiations; these are currently virtually duty-free and excluded from the mechanism. This measure is described as urgent but temporary, pending the introduction of an EU policy that restores competitiveness to Italian and European businesses without them having to rely on tariff protection.

articles.title: France and Germany move to exclude Moroccan-made cars from EU manufacturing incentives - HESPRESS English - Morocco News
articles.summary: France and Germany move to exclude Moroccan-made cars from EU manufacturing incentives  HESPRESS English - Morocco News
articles.full_text:
France and Germany have reached an agreement that could exclude cars manufactured in Morocco from preferential European Union subsidies and public procurement programs, potentially disadvantaging Renault and Stellantis factories that supply the European market, according to European automotive industry reporting and an analysis by the Jacques Delors Institute.
The agreement, announced on October 16, would favour vehicles produced within the EU and certain European partner countries, leaving Morocco and Turkey outside the proposed definition of “Made in Europe.”
The distinction matters because the proposed rules could determine which manufacturers benefit from public financial support as Europe seeks to strengthen its automotive industry against growing Chinese competition. They would not prohibit Moroccan-made vehicles from entering the EU market.
The Franco-German compromise links two previously contested issues: European manufacturing preferences and the bloc’s 2035 emissions requirements for new cars.
Germany secured French support for relaxing the proposed emissions target to a 90% reduction, while France obtained German backing for a narrower definition of European production, according to Agence Europe.
The agreement is intended to influence negotiations over the Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed by the European Commission in March.
The legislation would introduce European-content and low-carbon requirements into selected public procurement contracts and subsidy programmes, including those covering vehicles, steel and clean technologies.
Morocco’s potential exclusion has raised questions about its place in European automotive supply chains.
Renault operates major factories in Tangier and Casablanca, while Stellantis manufactures vehicles in Kenitra. Their production networks link Moroccan facilities with European manufacturers and suppliers.
Guillaume Duval, an adviser to the Jacques Delors Institute, criticized the compromise in an October 27 analysis, arguing that excluding Morocco and Turkey could undermine Europe’s efforts to develop competitive production networks closer to home.
Duval said European manufacturers need lower-cost neighbouring production bases to compete with Chinese companies, particularly in markets outside Europe.
The exclusion could also conflict with the EU’s stated objective of strengthening economic integration with Mediterranean partners, he argued.

articles.title: UK Defence Secretary warns Putin may yet turn on NATO - UK Defence Journal
articles.summary: UK Defence Secretary warns Putin may yet turn on NATO  UK Defence Journal
articles.full_text:
Britain has to invest and has to be ready because President Putin is waging a war in Europe while saying he has no interest in one, the Defence Secretary has said, describing investment in capability, in the defence industrial base and in alliances as the things that make war less likely, according to remarks made to reporters in Glasgow.
Wes Streeting was speaking at BAE Systems Scotstoun, where a new offsets policy was announced. Asked by this publication what his warning that Britain has around a thousand days to be ready to fight and win a war means for the armed forces and for the public, and what sacrifices the public are being asked to make to get there, he said: “Well, we’re investing in our capability, we’re investing in our defence industrial base, and we’re investing in our alliances. Those things make us stronger, and the stronger we are, the stronger our deterrence, and the less likely we are to find ourselves at war.
“We don’t seek confrontation with Russia. We have no quarrel with the Russian people. But what we can’t avoid is the hard reality that at the same time that President Putin says he’s not interested in war in Europe, he’s currently waging one, and he gave the Ukrainians those assurances that he had no plans to invade only weeks before the Russian invasion took place.
“So in that climate, we have to invest. We have to be ready. And in terms of what we’re asking of the country, as the Chancellor’s Budget showed this week, we are asking people to make that contribution right across government, and so defence is our number one duty, our number one priority, and that’s why it’s my responsibility to make sure that every penny that goes in is well spent, and that every bit of value we can extract for jobs and growth here in Scotland and right across the United Kingdom is realised. That’s my commitment.”
The contribution he describes falls across government and therefore on departmental budgets, and his answer turned on deterrence, which holds that a force strong enough to make an attack unprofitable is a force that never has to fight.
He was speaking after the announcement of a new offsets policy, under which overseas companies winning British defence contracts worth more than £50 million can be required to put benefits back into the country worth up to the full value of the contract, through jobs, apprenticeships, factories, investment in British suppliers or transfers of technology. A central Offset Authority will agree, value and monitor each arrangement, and the policy applies to a select number of procurements from April 2027. Ministers consulted industry on the approach earlier this year.
Asked what role Scotland will play in the Defence Investment Plan, John Healey, who moved from defence to the Treasury and delivered Wednesday’s Budget as Chancellor, said: “Defence is our number one priority. We also announced today the defence secretary and policy, where people have seen this is a government that will direct our defence investment first and foremost in British jobs and British businesses. But there will be things that we need to buy from abroad and from allies.
“So Norwegians, for instance, are part procuring some of this portion behind us, and they will require us because they have a policy that we’re now introducing for the first time ever in Britain, which we call an offset policy. We will buy some of the things the Norwegians produce that we can’t here.
“Now, in future, when Britain places contracts abroad, we’ll make sure that those we place those contracts with invest in Britain as well, jobs, business support, innovation, so that we can make sure that every pound of British taxpayers’ money works twice.”
Norway ordered five Type 26 frigates from Britain in a £10 billion deal supporting 2,000 jobs on the Clyde, and Oslo has run an industrial cooperation requirement of its own for decades, obliging foreign suppliers of significant equipment to place work with Norwegian firms. More than £35.2 billion has been spent with overseas industry since 2016, eleven per cent of direct departmental expenditure with industry and commerce, while 85 per cent already goes to British firms.
Streeting also attacked the Scottish National Party’s position on nuclear weapons, responding to the First Minister’s claim that the government is leaving Scotland short of defence. He said: “We’ve got HMS Prince of Wales currently out on a major exercise now, so I think it’s very visible proof that what the First Minister said is both irresponsible and unfounded. I don’t think the SNP should be playing party politics with national defence and security.
“In terms of the risk of leaving the UK with insufficient defence, one of the biggest risks facing that security is the SNP’s position on unilateral nuclear disarmament. It is by far and away the most important deterrent that we have, and it’s not just the UK’s deterrent, it’s NATO’s deterrent. So any time the SNP says that a separate Scotland can be a NATO member, they have to first explain how their white flag policy on unilateral nuclear disarmament would work under a nuclear alliance.”
The party voted narrowly in 2012 to drop its opposition to NATO membership while keeping its opposition to nuclear weapons, a position that would require an independent Scotland to join an alliance whose strategic concept describes nuclear weapons as the supreme guarantee of allied security, while removing the British deterrent from Faslane and Coulport. New members are admitted by unanimous agreement of the existing ones.
Asked whether Scotland is a target for Russia, Streeting said: “The people of Scotland and people right across the United Kingdom can draw comfort and security in the knowledge that we have some extraordinary capability at our disposal. Across our armed forces, as well as our special forces, and the protection of the NATO alliance, and that principle that an attack on one is an attack on all.
“I don’t think that Putin would be foolish enough to seek a direct war with NATO today. What I can’t be certain of is that at some point in the future he might not try, and that’s NATO’s threat assessment, and that’s why we are building our capability, building our defence industry, including here in Scotland, and building our alliances so that we are strong and therefore able to deter any potential Russian threat.”
He added that governments across the United Kingdom and local councils should play their part in national resilience, work led by the Cabinet Office through the Home Defence Programme, whose public awareness campaign launched on 22 October.
Healey rejected the Scottish government’s claim that its budget is being cut by £650 million in real terms, telling reporters: “No, they’re wrong. The Scottish budget is bigger than it’s been before.”
The Budget set a target date of 2030 for defence spending to reach three per cent of gross domestic product, with the route to the NATO commitment of three and a half per cent by 2035 left to next year’s Spending Review, and the Defence Investment Plan is backed by £298 billion over four years. The Scottish defence economy is worth £2.5 billion and directly supports 12,200 jobs, including 300 roles in Edinburgh on a £453 million Typhoon radar contract.

articles.title: EU accepts Temu’s action plan to remedy Digital Services Act breaches following €200m penalty - The News International
articles.summary: EU accepts Temu’s action plan to remedy Digital Services Act breaches following €200m penalty  The News International
articles.full_text:
Under a newly approved compliance roadmap, the cross-border e-commerce giant must overhaul its risk assessment protocols and crack down on illegal products within four months
The European Commission has officially accepted a corrective compliance roadmap submitted by cross-border e-commerce platform Temu.
The move follows a landmark €200 million fine levied against the company over systemic failures to curb the widespread sale of counterfeit, unsafe, and illegal products under the European Union's strict Digital Services Act (DSA).
The plan focuses on five measures to remedy the breach, and Temu now has four months to conduct an interim risk assessment, the EU regulator, said in a statement.
The five-point action plan:
Under the newly accepted framework, Temu is legally bound to overhaul its backend operations across five critical pillars such as:
Targeted risk analysis:
Factoring the specific vulnerabilities of its high-volume discount marketplace model into security evaluations.
Mitigation metrics:
Establishing verifiable benchmarks to track how effectively illicit listings are flagged and eliminated.
Content moderation audits:
Upgrading automated and human review systems that screen for banned merchandise.
Algorithmic accountability:
Scrutinizing recommendation engines to ensure platform algorithms do not actively promote unsafe or illegal items.
Seller exploitation defenses:
Closing loopholes that bad-faith merchants use to disguise or elevate problematic listings.
The Commission had imposed a €200 million ($224.08 million) fine on Temu in May for not doing enough to stop the sale of illegal products.
A spokesperson for Temu, which is owned by PDD Holdings, said it welcomed the Commission's approval of its plan under which the company will have to assess possible shortcomings of its content moderation system, among other steps.
Temu, along with Shein and other ecommerce platforms, has been hit by the EU imposing €3 fees on low-value ecommerce packages since the start of July.
Parcels worth less than €150 previously entered the bloc duty-free.
Regulators previously found that Temu's platform safeguards and risk assessment procedures were fundamentally inadequate, allowing dangerous goods such as non-compliant electrical chargers and children's toys exceeding chemical safety limits—to easily reach European consumers.

articles.title: US senator briefed on Trump's plans to restart Iran war says proposal is 'insane' - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: US senator briefed on Trump's plans to restart Iran war says proposal is 'insane'  Middle East EyeU.S. Warns Gulf of Possible Short, Intense Renewal of Iran War After Midterms  WSJUS weighs new Iran strikes as Vance reaches out: Is war or a deal closer?  Al JazeeraTrump plans to resume strikes on Iran day after midterm elections  MS NOWMilitary choices for Iran are being readied for president as midterm elections loom: officials  Fox News
articles.full_text:
Senator Chris Murphy says he has been briefed on the US's plan to restart the war on Iran, calling it "insane" and saying it would lead to a "devastating escalation".
"You've heard a preview that it would be a short-duration plan. I'll just say this: their plan is insane," Murphy said, speaking at an event organised by the Middle East Institute in Washington, DC, on Wednesday.
"It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law."
Murphy, a member of the Senate Foreign Relations and Appropriations committees, made the comments after American media reported on Wednesday that the US warned several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military offensive against Iran after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The warning sent by diplomatic and military channels is the latest indication that the US and Israel are preparing to launch another round of attacks against Iran, in an effort to weaken Tehran and force it to negotiations, according to a report in The Wall Street Journal.
"There's been open reporting as to what we may be planning and the civilian infrastructure we may be targeting," Murphy said.
"They've been asked by the president to develop a plan - whether they believe it will work or not, I do not know. But the plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests.
"We are seeing the president ready another devastating military campaign after the election, just as illegal as the first iteration was at the time, where Americans are fed up with this war."
'The plan that they have developed will lead, in my view, to a prolongment and an escalation of this war that will be devastating for our security interests'
- Senator Chris Murphy
Murphy spoke at the Middle East Institute about his trip to Qatar and Saudi Arabia earlier this month, assessing the war's impact on the region.
He is the first Democratic senator to visit the region since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February. Murphy met with leaders including Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The WSJ reported that US forces have been restocking their munitions in the region, and bomber aircraft and jet fighters are preparing for attacks, according to officials.
It also reported that the US military is moving a Patriot missile defence system from Texas to Israel to support defences, according to flight-tracking data and two officials. The Patriot system includes radar equipment, missile launchers and interceptor missiles.
Next month, an aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine expeditionary unit will also join around 20 other warships operating in the Middle East, the report said.
Last week, the US press also reported that US troops and diplomats have been evacuating posts in the Middle East.
NBC News reported that the State Department ordered a further reduction in staff at diplomatic posts in the region.
'A cover-up'
Murphy said during his trip that he was part of a number of classified briefings and spoke to military leadership about the damage and "the reality" there.
"Our base in Bahrain is obliterated; it is not usable, and our base in Qatar is usable but at a much lower level capacity, and it is pretty clear that we still don't have the ability to protect any of our diplomats or our troops... right now," he said.
Murphy added that he saw first-hand the US's "cover-up" in hiding the cost of war.
"The trip was incredibly valuable, not just to get a sense of how rattled the entire region is, but to really see first-hand a cover-up that is underway, a dizzying and coordinated attempt to try to hide from the American people and from Congress the costs and the consequences of this war," he said.
"It's like nothing I've ever seen in my now 20 years in the United States Congress."
The Pentagon told Congress last week that the US-Israeli war on Iran, now in its eighth month, had cost the US $47.1bn through 16 October, a rise from the previous $37.5bn cited by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Bombs, missiles and other types of ammunition made up over 60 percent of the total costs.
US President Donald Trump hasn't made a final decision yet, but is inclined towards launching a major attack that could target Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to several reports.
"We may do another little Epic Fury," Trump said at a rally in Florida last week, using the US military's term for its war on Iran.

Vice President JD Vance is facing backlash after responding to a young voter's question about housing affordability with an off-topic joke about Ohio Senator Jon Husted's rear.
The exchange unfolded Thursday during a Fox News town hall at Texas Christian University, where student Kate White, vice president of the school's Turning Point USA chapter, pressed Vance on how young Americans could afford to start a life amid soaring housing costs.
“How does the right and yourself expect us to start families young when you know the average price of a home in America now costs more than $415,000, which just feels out of reach for us,” White asked.
Vance thanked White for the question before diverting to Husted, the Republican senator from Ohio who previously held Vance's Senate seat.
“I want to point out that I think that I've been asked four or maybe five questions by my count, I've only been asked one question about Jon Husted's a** and it was by Jesse Watters,” Vance said about the Fox News host, who moderated the town hall.
Watters laughed at Vance’s response and said it was what people were talking about.
"Maybe you should run for Senate on the Democratic side here in Texas, Jesse,” Vance said.
After the joke, Vance acknowledged that Republicans had not done enough to address the financial pressures facing younger Americans.
“Most Republicans don't… I think that I'm an exception,” he said, adding that he believed President Donald Trump was focused on restoring the American dream and making homeownership more attainable.
Vance attributed rising housing costs partly to undocumented immigration under previous administrations and home purchases by Wall Street firms and foreign investors. He also claimed Texas home listing prices had fallen 2.5 percent, following a 100 percent increase under former President Joe Biden.
He then finally answered White’s question.
“My personal advice is one guy talking to a person who's been in similar shoes is it's never the right time, so go ahead and do it, because you're never going to regret getting married and having kids,” Vance told the student.
Watters agreed with Vance's advice, adding his own perspective: "And sometimes, you know, when you're in love, you just get pregnant, and you figure it out. That's not a great political answer, but it usually works well."
Vance’s off-topic quip about Husted's derriere comes amid a series of comments Trump has made about Husted's physique while campaigning for the Ohio senator, who is seeking election to a full Senate term on November 3.
Trump first made headlines with the remarks during an October 12 rally in Youngstown, Ohio, when he recalled examining Husted's body after learning the senator had been an All-American football player at the University of Dayton.
“I looked at his a**,” Trump told the crowd, before describing his legs, shoulders and hands.
Trump later repeated the comments at several campaign appearances, even suggesting his remarks had helped improve Husted's standing in the polls.
Like Trump, Vance is now facing backlash over the odd talking point.
Krystal Ball, a political commentator and podcast host, called it a “tone-deaf moment,” while former NASA astronaut Scott Kelly said the remark was “disgusting, but not surprising.”
The official X account for California Governor Gavin Newsom Press Office simply reacted to the clip with three question marks, while former Trump White House Press Secretary Sarah Matthews wrote: “I genuinely cannot believe this is a real exchange between a voter and the Vice President of the United States.”

articles.title: Healey’s budget cuts mean Britain is likely to miss green heating targets - The Guardian
articles.summary: Healey’s budget cuts mean Britain is likely to miss green heating targets  The GuardianWarm Homes Plan faces deeper cuts after UK budget  POLITICO.euI’m Britain’s biggest energy boss – scrapping help for heat pumps is a gift to Russia  The i PaperUK – Burnham’s first budget ends VAT relief for home solar  pv EuropeHeat pump demand jumped by 58% in October, research finds  Planning, Building & Construction Today
articles.full_text:
Britain is unlikely to hit its targets on green heating after the cuts announced by John Healey this week, experts have warned, as critics of Ed Miliband claim the former energy secretary’s green agenda is being dismantled.
The chancellor unveiled more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department’s budget this week, much of which will pay for higher defence spending.
One casualty of the cuts is the government’s scheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions are being undermined.
Some believe the cuts are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh. However, energy department sources insisted the government’s longer-term changes will incentivise people to move towards cleaner power sources and benefit the overall green agenda.
Andrew Sissons, a director at the research charity Nesta, said: “After the cuts announced on Wednesday, it is very difficult to see how we can hit our clean heating targets. It is even possible that a Labour government will be the first to miss the targets it has signed up to in the current carbon budget.”
Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments.
Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.
Under the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, and was planning to increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30.
The plan forms a key part of the UK’s programme to clean up its heating networks and hit its overall emissions reduction targets. However, ministers said on Wednesday the scheme’s funding would rise only in line with inflation, meaning the number of installations is likely to stagnate or rise much more slowly than previously planned.
“It’s disappointing – so frustrating,” said Ed Matthew, the director of the UK programme at the thinktank E3G. “We are behind a lot of other countries in rolling out heat pumps and we need a sea change in take-up to change that.”
The cuts to heat pump subsidies came alongside about £250m of other cuts to the warm homes plan, £500m worth of cuts to hydrogen schemes, and £200m to funding for carbon capture and storage technology – all projects once championed by Miliband.
Healey also announced that renewable projects would only be approved in future if they could be shown to bring costs down and were ready to be connected with the grid. Officials insist the government remains committed to its target of having clean power by 2030, though many experts believe that will be impossible under the new system.
One government source said: “This is probably the most significant shift we have seen in energy policy since we came to office. The emphasis now is on cost, not just building to make sure there is enough capacity to hit our green targets.”
Paul Ovenden, a former adviser to Keir Starmer, said: “It is fascinating to see the energy capital budgets being raided to fund defence – this is the bones of Ed Miliband’s project being picked clean.
“This was something that has been discussed in government before – but Miliband always won that argument. Now he’s not in that department any more, it’s happened.”
Ovenden added: “Had he not helped to oust Starmer and Reeves, he’d probably be in post still and it wouldn’t have been possible.”
But allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever. They pointed out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed.
They also said the government’s intention to change energy markets so electricity prices are no longer so attached to gas prices would help encourage consumers to move away from fossil fuels.
One source said: “Ed and Miatta have both made affordability their focus. It would be wrong to suggest that prioritising cost is in any way a shift away from the green agenda.”
A spokesperson for the energy department said: “Over the last two years, we have made considerable progress, thanks to the momentum of clean power 2030, seeing £110bn of private-sector investment announced and securing enough clean power for over 20m homes.
“We are committed to making the most of clean, homegrown power and meeting our heat pump target to protect consumers from volatile fossil fuel prices.”

articles.summary: UK vows defense spending boost by 2030 but dodges hard questions  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
LONDON — Britain's top finance minister on Wednesday promised an uplift in defense spending by 2030 to "set the direction" for meeting a crucial NATO target — but didn't lay out how the government will get there.
John Healey quit as U.K. defense secretary in the dying days of Keir Starmer's government in a row over funding. On Wednesday he gave his first budget as chancellor under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, setting out the government's tax and spending plans.
Healey committed for the first time to spending 3% of GDP on the nation's defenses by 2030 — something he had called for when he quit Starmer's administration. But he declined to say where he would find the money, a staging post on the way to meeting NATO's target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035. Instead, he said a broader review of government spending would address it next year.

articles.title: Germany set for record trade deficit with Asia-Pacific in 2026, report says - Yahoo Finance UK
articles.summary: Germany set for record trade deficit with Asia-Pacific in 2026, report says  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
By Maria Martinez
BERLIN, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Germany's trade deficit with Asia-Pacific is set to hit a record of nearly €146 billion ($163 billion) in 2026 as falling exports to China outweigh growing sales elsewhere in the region, according to a report by Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) seen by Reuters.
The figures highlight the growing challenge facing German exporters in China, once one of their most important overseas markets, as Chinese companies expand domestic production of advanced technology, machinery and electric vehicles.
Exports to 29 core Asia-Pacific economies are expected to fall 3.2% this year to €185.3 billion, while imports are forecast to rise 6.4% to €330.9 billion, the state-owned trade promotion agency said.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is visiting Japan, South Korea and Singapore from Monday to Friday. On Tuesday he called for European and Asian middle powers to build a strategic alliance in trade, technology and security.
CHINA'S WEAKER DEMAND HITS GERMAN EXPORTERS
China accounts for around half of Germany's goods trade with Asia-Pacific and has an outsized effect on the overall figures, GTAI said.
Excluding China, German exports to the region would grow by 2.8% in 2026, while the trade deficit with Asia-Pacific would narrow to just under €35 billion.
German machinery exports to China fell 18% in the first seven months of 2026 from a year earlier, according to the report. Automotive exports dropped 30% over the same period.
German car sales in China have nearly halved from a peak of more than 5 million vehicles, GTAI said, as local manufacturers gain ground in electric cars and benefit from control over battery supply chains.
INDIA, SOUTHEAST ASIA GAIN GROUND
India is becoming a more important market and supplier for German companies, GTAI said.
German exports to India have nearly doubled over the past decade, as have imports from the South Asian country.
Imports are also becoming more diversified. While clothing remains important, German companies are increasingly buying pharmaceutical products and machine components from India, the report said.
Japan remains a relatively stable market for German companies despite the yen's sharp fall against the euro and dollar over the past six years, which has eroded Japanese purchasing power.
GTAI expects German exports to the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to grow faster than imports in 2026, helped by aircraft deliveries.
Over the longer term, the region is becoming increasingly important as a source of electronics and electrical equipment, moving beyond its traditional role as a supplier of clothing and footwear.
($1 = 0.8961 euros)
(Reporting by Maria Martinez and Christian Kraemer. Editing by Mark Potter)

articles.title: EDITORIAL: Trade with EU means higher carbon taxes - Yahoo News Canada
articles.summary: EDITORIAL: Trade with EU means higher carbon taxes  Yahoo News Canada
articles.full_text:
See more Toronto Sun on Google — save as a Preferred Source
Canadians will pay higher carbon taxes in trade with the European Union starting next year because of the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) — a carbon tariff on certain goods imported from Canada.
That's because the EU is imposing carbon tariffs on countries with lower carbon prices that those in the EU, primarily in the trade of metals.
Canada's current industrial carbon price is $95 per tonne of emissions, rising to $130 in 2035.
The EU's current carbon price in Canadian dollars is about $139 per tonne, already higher than what Canada plans for 2035.
In 2035, the EU's carbon price will be more than double Canada's $130 per tonne — estimated at close to $300 per tonne.
Th EU policy, starting next year, will enforce CBAMs on imports from countries that aren't linked to or fall under the EU's carbon market known as the Emissions Trading System.
Canada could presumably obtain an exemption from these new carbon tariffs if, through negotiations with the EU, it joins its carbon market and raises its carbon price to EU levels as part of establishing "an ever closer" association with the EU.
Without that, the EU would presumably impose an industrial carbon price next year based on the difference in Canada's carbon price, which will be $100 per tonne of emissions, compared to an estimated $139 to $156 per tonne in the EU.
In either case, there will be higher costs for Canadian consumers and the impacted sectors of our economy.
According to internal Global Affairs documents obtained by the CBC through an access to information request, initially only a relatively small amount of Canadian exports would be impacted by the EU's carbon tariffs, although it would obviously increase over time.
Their current value is estimated at $2.8 billion, 7.4% of Canada's trade with the EU, although the lion's share will impact Canada's aluminum and iron and steel sectors, already hard hit by U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs.
The economies of Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador would take the hardest hit initially, according to the documents.
During last year's federal election, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he planned to impose carbon tariffs on foreign goods imported into Canada, but has not implemented such a policy up to now.

articles.title: ECB Holds Interest Rates at 2.5% as Euro Zone Inflation Hits 3.8% - Cirebon Times
articles.summary: ECB Holds Interest Rates at 2.5% as Euro Zone Inflation Hits 3.8%  Cirebon Times
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank kept its key deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, as rising energy costs pushed euro zone inflation to 3.8%. The Governing Council maintained its wait-and-see approach after September's rate increase, citing uncertainty over inflation and economic growth despite mounting pressure on borrowing costs.
The decision followed a 25-basis-point increase in September. According to the ECB, higher energy prices pose an upside risk to inflation while potentially weakening economic growth, although underlying inflation and wage growth have remained broadly stable.
Euro zone inflation reached 3.8% in September, its highest level since September 2023, while energy price inflation climbed to 18.8% amid continued turmoil in the Middle East. According to LSEG data, financial markets priced in a 67% probability of another rate increase in December following the announcement.
ECB President Christine Lagarde said the central bank had not observed additional inflationary effects beyond those already incorporated into its September projections. She identified rising costs across oil, gasoline, fuel, natural gas and refining margins as major developments since the previous policy meeting.
Lagarde also highlighted a sharp increase in long-term financing costs, with average 10-year sovereign bond yields rising by approximately 35 basis points. She said the Governing Council unanimously concluded that holding rates was appropriate given the uncertainty and broadly unchanged underlying inflation.
"At this point in time we are not seeing second round effects in addition to what is already included in the projections" released in September, ECB President Christine Lagarde told CNBC's Annette Weisbach during a press conference.
The ECB said the euro zone economy continued expanding in the third quarter, supported by a recovery in services since the Middle East conflict began. Investment related to artificial intelligence is also supporting manufacturing, digital services and exports, while government spending on infrastructure and defense is sustaining business activity.
However, the central bank warned that higher energy prices could weaken consumer confidence as increased financing costs weigh on economic growth. Lagarde also said the ECB would continue monitoring rising French borrowing costs and growing fragmentation in financial markets.
She attributed the broader increase in long-term borrowing costs partly to inflation and interest rate expectations, as well as increased bond issuance by large technology companies. She noted that these companies were issuing more long-term debt, intensifying competition for financing.
Deutsche Bank's chief European economist, Mark Wall, said the outlook for ECB monetary policy had become more difficult to predict. He questioned whether previous rate increases and tighter financial conditions would be sufficient to contain the risk of further energy-driven inflation.
"Predicting the path of ECB monetary policy is becoming more challenging," Deutsche Bank's chief European economist, Mark Wall, said in a note on Thursday.
Wall said the two rate increases already delivered and the tightening of financial conditions since September might not be enough to counter the additional inflation risk posed by energy prices. He also raised questions about how Lagarde's announced departure as ECB president could affect policy decisions next year.
Wall said Deutsche Bank expected another increase before the end of the year, taking the deposit rate to 2.75% in December while Lagarde remained president. He added that this would probably mark the end of the rate-hiking cycle.
"One question is whether the two hikes already delivered and the tightening of financial conditions since September are enough to lean against the further increase in energy inflation risk? Probably not." Wall said.
Dean Turner, chief euro zone and U.K. economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, also viewed the ECB's decision as a pause rather than the end of monetary tightening. He said France's fiscal challenges were unlikely to change the policy direction unless broader financial stress emerged.
"The ECB's focus remains firmly on ensuring that today's energy-driven inflation does not develop into a more persistent problem." Turner said.

articles.full_text:
Rising energy costs and mounting borrowing expenses have complicated the euro zone's inflation outlook, prompting the European Central Bank (ECB) to maintain its key deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, October 29, 2026. The decision followed a 25-basis-point increase in September and came as inflation reached its highest level since September 2023.
The ECB's Governing Council said underlying inflation and wage growth remained broadly stable, allowing policymakers to wait despite growing economic risks. The bank warned that higher energy prices could push inflation upward while simultaneously weighing on economic growth.
According to LSEG data, money markets priced in a 67% probability of another interest rate increase in December following the announcement. Economists at Deutsche Bank and UBS Global Wealth Management also considered further tightening possible as policymakers seek to prevent energy-driven inflation from becoming persistent.
ECB President Christine Lagarde told CNBC's Annette Weisbach that policymakers had not observed additional inflationary pressures spreading beyond those already reflected in the bank's September projections.
"At this point in time we are not seeing second round effects in addition to what is already included in the projections" released in September, Lagarde said.
Lagarde identified higher costs for oil, gasoline, fuel and natural gas, along with increased refining margins, as major developments since the previous policy meeting. She also highlighted a sharp increase in long-term financing costs, with the average 10-year sovereign bond yield rising by around 35 basis points.
She said the Governing Council had considered whether another increase was appropriate but ultimately agreed unanimously to maintain the current rate, citing uncertainty and broadly unchanged underlying inflation.
"If you combine these two factors — actually, the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate — but on the basis of the uncertainty that accumulates and that rises as well, on the basis of underlying inflation that has broadly remained unchanged, the Governing Council unanimously decided that we were well positioned enough at this stage to hold and that a measured approach at this point in time remained appropriate," Lagarde said.
Euro zone headline inflation reached 3.8% in September, its highest level since September 2023, while energy price inflation climbed to 18.8% amid continuing instability in the Middle East. The resurgence in energy prices following the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February had prompted the ECB to raise rates in June for the first time since 2023.
Despite these pressures, the Governing Council said the euro zone economy continued to expand in the third quarter. Services had recovered since the conflict began, while artificial intelligence-related investment supported manufacturing, digital services and exports. Government spending on infrastructure and defense also contributed to business activity, although higher energy bills and financing costs threatened consumer confidence and growth.
Lagarde also said the ECB would continue monitoring rising borrowing costs in France and increasing fragmentation in financial markets. She attributed the global increase in long-term yields partly to inflation and interest rate expectations, as well as debt issuance by large technology companies seeking long-term financing.
Deutsche Bank's chief European economist, Mark Wall, said the outlook for ECB monetary policy had become increasingly difficult to predict.
"Predicting the path of ECB monetary policy is becoming more challenging," Wall said.
Wall questioned whether the two rate increases already delivered and the tightening of financial conditions since September would be sufficient to counter rising energy-related inflation risks.
"One question is whether the two hikes already delivered and the tightening of financial conditions since September are enough to lean against the further increase in energy inflation risk? Probably not," Wall said.
Wall also identified uncertainty surrounding Lagarde's announced departure from the ECB presidency as a potential factor affecting policy decisions next year. He said Deutsche Bank expected another increase before the end of the year.
"We think the institution is bigger than the person, but there's uncertainty. We expect one more hike to 2.75% in December while Lagarde is still President, and that's probably the end of the hiking cycle," Wall said.
Dean Turner, chief euro zone and U.K. economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, characterized the ECB's decision as a pause rather than a definitive end to interest rate increases.
"The ECB's focus remains firmly on ensuring that today's energy-driven inflation does not develop into a more persistent problem," Turner said.
Turner also said France's fiscal challenges were unlikely to alter the direction of monetary policy without broader financial stress.

articles.title: "Annual Cap of 350,000 Vehicles": China Concedes on Hybrid Exports Under EU Trade Pressure, Faces Difficulties Finding Alternative Markets and Expanding Local Production - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: "Annual Cap of 350,000 Vehicles": China Concedes on Hybrid Exports Under EU Trade Pressure, Faces Difficulties Finding Alternative Markets and Expanding Local Production  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
EU summit expected to discuss trade imbalance with China and responses to damage to European industry
China remains optimistic despite hybrid export restrictions, but market doubts persist
Chinese automakers expand European production, facing burdens from production costs and local sourcing rules
Trade relations with China are expected to emerge as a central agenda item at the European Union (EU) summit. As a widening trade imbalance deepens tensions between the two sides, international attention is turning to the EU's next steps. China has recently made some concessions amid the heightened trade tensions, including agreeing to limit hybrid vehicle exports. However, weak domestic demand and high barriers to alternative export markets suggest that reducing its dependence on Europe in the short term will be difficult.
EU Grapples With Trade Deficit With China
According to Reuters on the 14th (all dates hereafter are local time), leaders of the EU's 27 member states will meet in Brussels, Belgium, on the 15th–16th to discuss damage to European industries from a surge in imports of Chinese vehicles and manufactured goods, as well as potential trade responses. The EU's goods trade deficit with China reached EUR 360 billion (about USD 419 billion) last year and EUR 200 billion (about USD 233 billion) in the first half of this year. These deficits extend beyond automobiles, previously the main source of friction between the two sides, to manufacturing sectors including machinery, textiles, basic metals and chemicals. Concerns are consequently growing over weakening competitiveness among European companies and declining employment.
Against this backdrop, the European Commission's policy direction is shifting toward curbing the influx of Chinese products into the bloc. A prominent example is the imposition of high tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The Commission conducted an anti-subsidy investigation into Chinese EVs for about a year beginning in 2023. In July 2024, it imposed provisional countervailing duties after determining that Chinese government subsidies had distorted competition in the European market. This marked the first large-scale trade sanctions against Chinese EVs. In October of the same year, following approval from member states, the EU finalized additional tariffs of up to 35.3% on Chinese EVs, with rates varying by manufacturer. These duties are imposed on top of the existing 10% vehicle import tariff and are set to apply for five years from October 30, 2024.
Limits on Imports of Chinese Hybrids
Under this trade pressure, China has recently sought to ease tensions by offering some concessions in negotiations with the EU. On the 12th, the Financial Times (FT) reported that the Commission was pursuing a plan to cap annual imports of Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles at 350,000. This follows an agreement reached during trade talks held in Beijing, China, on the 8th–9th involving EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, among others. The import restrictions are scheduled to take effect in December this year, setting an annual import ceiling of 350,000 vehicles in 2027 and increasing it by 6% each year from 2028 through 2030.
The restrictions cover hybrids manufactured in China and exported to the EU, including vehicles made by European automakers at their Chinese factories. However, Chinese-brand vehicles produced within the EU will not be subject to the import cap. The EU estimates that China's hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc will reach about 800,000 this year. It calculates that the agreement could reduce imports of Chinese hybrids by more than half and lower their share of the European market from about 6% currently to around 3%.
China Confident Agreement Will "Actually Expand Exports"
China, by contrast, argues that the agreement has created opportunities for its companies to expand exports. In an official explanatory statement released on the 12th, China's Ministry of Commerce said, "According to Eurostat, EU imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles totaled 107,000 in 2024 and rose to 302,000 in 2025," adding, "The two sides agreed to expand imports from the 2025 level, ensuring export capacity and stable growth for Chinese companies." While the EU emphasized the reduction in imports relative to this year's projected volume, China highlighted the potential to expand future exports compared with last year's actual imports of 302,000 vehicles.
China's Ministry of Commerce also explained that the hybrid vehicle trade agreement follows three principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination and compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules. On non-discrimination in particular, it stated, "No measure should target only Chinese products or discriminate against Chinese companies," and noted that "the import quota allocated to China will be no smaller than the volume allocated to any other country from which the EU imports." Regarding compliance with WTO rules, it said, "China retains all rights within the WTO framework, including initiating dispute settlement proceedings and seeking trade compensation."
Table 1. Plan to Restrict Imports of Chinese Hybrids and the Two Sides' Positions
| Category | Key Details | 
|---|---|
| Import Restriction Plan | Set the annual import cap for Chinese hybrids at 350,000 vehicles in 2027, increasing it by 6% annually from 2028 through 2030 | 
| EU Position | A measure to cut imports of Chinese hybrids by more than half compared with this year's projected volume and reduce their market share | 
| China's Position | An agreement favorable to export expansion and stable growth, as the quota exceeds last year's actual import volume | 
Difficulties Finding Alternative Markets
Market doubts about China's optimism nevertheless persist. Observers warn that China is likely to struggle to redirect vehicles previously exported to Europe to other markets. For a start, demand in China's domestic auto market remains sluggish amid weak consumer sentiment and reduced purchase subsidies. According to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), domestic passenger car sales in September totaled about 1.63 million vehicles, down 28.1% year on year and marking the 12th consecutive monthly decline. Barriers to alternative export markets are also rising. After imposing an additional 100% tariff on Chinese EVs, the United States has tightened regulations on Chinese connected-car software and hardware, effectively blocking market access. Mexico also approved legislation last December imposing tariffs of up to 50% on some 1,400 product categories, including automobiles, imported from countries without free trade agreements (FTAs), such as China. Brazil raised tariffs on imported EVs and hybrids to 35% in July.
Existing major export markets also have limited capacity to absorb more vehicles. According to an automotive market report released in March by global accounting firm PwC, China's exports of passenger cars and light commercial vehicles (LVs) to Russia totaled about 556,000 last year, plunging 46% from a year earlier. This reflected a combination of adverse factors, including increases in Russia's import-related taxes and slowing local vehicle demand. Southeast Asia, which China is targeting as a new export hub, is also a relatively small market. According to PwC, vehicle sales across six major ASEAN countries—Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam and Singapore—totaled only about 3.5 million last year, while Chinese automakers held a market share of just 11%.
Effectiveness of Local Production Strategy Remains Uncertain
Against this backdrop, Chinese companies are stepping up efforts to establish local production and supply chains in Europe to find a way forward. In an interview with French business broadcaster BFM Business on the 12th, BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li said the company planned to secure two additional production sites in Europe and was considering France as a leading candidate. BYD has already built its first European vehicle assembly plant in Hungary and plans to begin full-scale operations in the fourth quarter of this year. Meanwhile, XPeng continues contract manufacturing at Magna International's Austrian plant and is examining options to partner with local manufacturers to build new factories or use existing facilities. Changan Automobile has also announced a target of expanding its European production capacity to 180,000 vehicles annually by 2028 and 350,000 by 2030.
The problem is that expanding local production in Europe may not necessarily strengthen Chinese companies' competitiveness. They must shoulder higher labor and energy costs than in China, while establishing new local parts supply chains also entails additional spending. Another uncertainty is that the EU's industrial regulatory direction has yet to be finalized. The Commission is currently pursuing stronger local production and parts sourcing requirements for products such as EVs through the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), while member states and industry debate what should qualify as European-made. Controversy continues over whether vehicles and components produced in non-EU countries such as Türkiye, the United Kingdom and Morocco should be recognized as European-made. Chinese automakers therefore risk having to make further adjustments to their parts sourcing networks and production systems depending on the rules ultimately adopted.

articles.title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine - BBC
articles.summary: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine  BBCUkraine’s Zelenskyy praises US over $2.1bn Patriot missile deal but warns it could take years  The GuardianUS greenlights $2.1bn sale of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine  Financial TimesUS approves potential $2.1 billion sale of scarce Patriot missiles to Ukraine  CNNNATO top commander sees no delays in delivery of Patriot missiles to Ukraine  Ukrinform
articles.full_text:
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks.
However Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.
The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.
The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.
Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.
In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies which his country was running critically low on.
In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".
He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.
It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.
Additional reporting by Victoria Bourne

articles.title: 7th EU Competition Law Conference: Algorithmic Pricing, DMA, Mergers & Digital Markets - Crowell & Moring LLP
articles.summary: 7th EU Competition Law Conference: Algorithmic Pricing, DMA, Mergers & Digital Markets  Crowell & Moring LLP
articles.full_text:
Client Alert | 7 min read | 10.29.26
Introduction
On 8 October 2026, Crowell & Moring, King’s College London, and the Competition Law Center at George Washington University co-hosted the 7th EU Competition Law Conference at De Warande in Brussels. Mark Meador, Commissioner at the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC), delivered the opening keynote address, followed by four panels bringing together practitioners, regulators, academics, and in-house counsel to discuss the latest developments in EU, UK, and US competition law enforcement. Among other things, the panels examined algorithmic pricing; the European Commission’s (Commission) new guidelines on exclusionary abuses under Article 102 TFEU (Article 102 Guidelines); the impact of dominant positions in merger reviews; and lessons from the enforcement of the Digital Markets Act (DMA) and the UK’s Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act.
Keynote Speech – FTC Commissioner Mark Meador
Commissioner Meador highlighted the common origins of US and European competition law enforcement and argued that today’s interconnected economies make international cooperation essential, but that increasingly divergent approaches on either side of the Atlantic risk undermining convergence and collaboration.
On US enforcement, he asserted that predictability comes from consistent case-by-case application of established principles, not detailed ex ante rules for every emerging technology.
Although enforcement actions involving dominant firms often take too long, accelerated timelines and case management orders can deliver relief sooner without abandoning case-by-case analysis.
Intervention should address proven harm proportionately without deterring lawful conduct.
He questioned whether ex ante digital regulation provides the desired clarity, timely relief, or harm-based intervention.
Broad obligations and substantial fines, he argued, create uncertainty: Apple delayed the rollout of features in the EU in 2024, including Apple Intelligence and iPhone Mirroring, citing DMA interoperability requirements.
With six of seven designated gatekeepers and 22 of 23 designated services American, he warned that uneven burdens could erode trust.
On procedural fairness and content moderation, Meador contrasted targeted US action against proven unfair or deceptive practices with the Digital Services Act’s (DSA) broader approach.
He raised concerns about lawful speech and procedural fairness, citing allegations that the Commission had allowed insufficient time to review large volumes of documents and had imposed restrictive conditions on that review.
Companies, he stressed, need clear notice, defined deadlines, reasonable response periods, and even-handed enforcement.

Looking ahead, Meador advocated cooperation grounded in evidence, proportional remedies, non-discrimination, due process, sovereignty, and comity. Collaboration between the EU and US competition law systems should be driven by convergence, even if national priorities or methods differ.
The full speech has been published on the website of the FTC and can be found here.
Panel 1 – The Invisible Cartel: Detecting and Prosecuting Technology-Enabled Coordination
Panel Chair: Alison Jones (Professor of Law, King’s College London). Panellists: Ilaria Fanton (Principal, Oxera Consulting); Renato Nazzini KC (Barrister, Monckton Chambers and Professor of Law, King’s College London); Jason Murray (Partner, Crowell & Moring).
Pricing algorithms can facilitate more stable coordination by improving the monitoring of rivals’ prices and the speed and credibility of retaliation. EU and UK horizontal guidelines address algorithmic pricing. The Commission identifies four scenarios: algorithmic monitoring of an existing cartel; agreement to use a common algorithm (“collusion by code”); hub-and-spoke coordination through a shared platform; and the use of independent algorithms relying on public information, which is in principle lawful. The UK posters case illustrated the risk: firms unable to coordinate frequent price changes manually achieved near-perfect alignment overnight using pricing software. On liability, EU guidance treats algorithms as firms’ agents, emphasising that pricing practices that are illegal offline remain illegal when implemented online. Personalised pricing primarily raises transparency concerns; several national authorities have secured disclosure commitments.
In the US, litigation spans multiple sectors. The US Department of Justice’s (DOJ) first major rental-software case and divergent recent Ninth and Third Circuit decisions highlight uncertainty. Withdrawal of the FTC’s information-sharing “safety zone” guidelines in 2023 left a guidance gap, while New York and California adopted legislative responses.
Panel 2 – Gatekeeper, Monopolist, or Dominant? Unilateral Conduct in a Complex Regulatory Landscape
Panel Chair: Thomas De Meese (Partner, Crowell & Moring). Panellists: Damien Gerard (Prosecutor General, Belgian Competition Authority (BCA)); Geneviève Borremans (Senior Legal Counsel Competition Law, Euroclear); Liza Lovdahl-Gormsen (Senior Research Fellow, British Institute of International and Comparative Law); Andy Gavil (Senior Of Counsel, Crowell & Moring; Professor of Law at Howard University).
The Commission’s Article 102 Guidelines seek a workable effects-based approach following the Intel cases without reverting to formalism. A dedicated section on objective justification addresses efficiencies, but companies retain the burden of proof under a sliding scale, making defences difficult in practice. In-house counsel welcomed clearer frameworks for margin squeeze, tying, and refusal to supply, as well as the reaffirmation that dominance is unlikely below a 40% market share. Uncertain boundaries may chill investment and pro-competitive conduct. The UK Competition and Markets Authority’s (CMA) shift towards ex ante powers has coincided with limited Chapter 2 public enforcement and increased private litigation before the Competition Appeal Tribunal. A proposed “reverse follow-on” mechanism would allow the CMA to use private liability findings to impose behavioural or structural remedies. EU and US unilateral-conduct approaches show more convergence than is often assumed, with causation, de facto tying, and efficiencies litigated on both sides.
On AI, the panel highlighted “small tech” enforcement by national competition authorities such as the BCA against domestic gatekeepers, focusing, for example, on data portability (such as user profiles) between companies. Whether pre-emptive intervention is warranted absent established dominance or collusion remains unresolved. Existing tying and bundling frameworks are difficult to apply to digital products, although the Guidelines’ principles may support approaches to de facto tying and exclusivity.
Panel 3 – The Dealmaker’s Dilemma: Navigating a New Era of Merger Scrutiny
Panel Chair: Marieke Van Nieuwenborgh (Partner, Crowell & Moring). Panellists: Marta Janek-Jecker (Case Handler, DG Competition, Commission); Joost Vandenbossche (Principal, RBB Economics); Peter Broadhurst (Partner, Crowell & Moring); Rebecca Valentine (Partner, Crowell & Moring, formerly a Trial Attorney for the DOJ’s Antitrust Division).
The Commission’s April 2026 Draft Merger Guidelines attracted approximately 200 responses. They codify case law and adopt a forward-looking approach encompassing innovation and resilience alongside price. The panel welcomed the “innovation shield” for small innovative companies and acceptance of dynamic efficiencies. US guidelines, issued in 2023, could address innovation more fully, but claims require supporting evidence and consistent transaction documents. Economists cautioned that demanding efficiency standards structurally disadvantage those arguments relative to theories of harm.
In Booking/eTraveli, the General Court accepted that an increase in hotel-booking market share of 1% or less could significantly impede effective competition given Booking’s existing dominance. Dominance is regaining prominence: the Draft Guidelines recognise reduced market contestability as a theory of harm where one party is dominant. Paramount/Warner Bros. illustrated divergence: the DOJ closed its investigation, while US states raised concerns over negotiating leverage and reduced output. The Commission’s conditional clearance in the EU addressed film-distribution concerns in several Member States through a structural remedy. The package reflected a trend towards structural commitments with significant behavioural measures. Both the Commission and DOJ show greater openness to behavioural remedies, which should be practicable to administer and supported by clear metrics and reporting. New thresholds, call-in powers, novel theories of harm, and proliferating foreign direct investment (FDI) and national security regimes further complicate merger review.
Fireside Chat – From Rules to Reality: What Comes Next for Digital Markets?
Panel Chairs: Andrew Gavil (Senior Of Counsel, Crowell & Moring; Professor of Law, Howard University School of Law); Bill Kovacic (Global Competition Professor of Law and Policy, George Washington University Law School). Panellists: Lucia Bonova (Head of Unit, DG Comp, European Commission); Mike Walker (formerly CMA / Frontier Economics & University of Durham).
The discussion compared the DMA with the UK’s Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act, focusing on implementation, remedies, and AI. DMA enforcement has taken longer than expected but has accelerated: cases concerning Google’s steering and self-preferencing practices resulted in fines, two Article 6 specification decisions were issued in respect of Google, and market investigations into Amazon AWS and Microsoft Azure as possible gatekeepers are nearing completion. The panel described AI as the only digital sector without entrenched market power, offering a window for genuine ex ante intervention. Implementa
