articles.title: EUROMETAL: Carbon Costs Undermine the Competitiveness of European Producers in Export Markets - Металлургпром
articles.summary: EUROMETAL: Carbon Costs Undermine the Competitiveness of European Producers in Export Markets  Металлургпром
articles.full_text:
EUROMETAL President Alexander M. Julius said at the Steel Networking Summit 2026 that the gap between EU measures on steel imports and trading conditions for finished goods containing steel is undermining the competitiveness of European producers. He said a level playing field must be ensured at every stage of the steel production chain.
Speaking at the Steel Networking Summit 2026, organized in Istanbul by the Turkish Steel Exporters’ Association (ÇİB), Julius discussed trade measures in the European steel market, imports of steel-containing products and the impact of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) on manufacturing.
According to Julius, over the past 25 years the EU has imposed anti-dumping measures, countervailing duties and safeguards on steel imports. Meanwhile, industries that use steel in manufacturing have not received comparable protection from imports of finished goods. He said this difference in conditions for steel producers and companies that use steel should be taken into account when assessing the decline in steel demand in Europe.
Gap in protection for steel and steel-containing products
Julius’s presentation said the EU’s duty-free steel import quota is 18.3 million tonnes and covers 30 product categories. From July 1, 2026, imports above the quota will be subject to a 50% duty. Other steel market protection tools cited included anti-dumping duties and countervailing measures against subsidies.
For many industrial goods containing steel, standard Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) duty rates range from 0% to 2.7%. Such products are not subject to general safeguard quotas comparable to those on steel, and trade measures apply only to specific goods.
The presentation also noted that, at the end of 2025, around one-third of the 232 trade defence measures in force in the EU concerned iron and steel.
Julius said that protection measures and carbon costs on steel inputs are rising, while European companies that use steel compete with finished products imported at low tariff rates. He said this is increasing pressure on steel-consuming industries.
Industrial weakness also affects steel demand
Julius stressed the importance of preserving the competitiveness of steel-buying manufacturers. Protecting steelmaking alone does not solve problems arising further down the production chain, he said.
Higher steel prices and carbon costs are intended to encourage investment in low-carbon production, Julius noted. However, if competitive conditions with imported steel-containing products are not balanced, this will place an additional burden on European industry.
He added that weak demand for steel in Europe cannot be considered separately from the loss of market share by industries that use it.
Goods previously sent to the US and Canada are being redirected to the EU
According to Julius, US and Canadian trade measures affect not only direct steel trade but also shipments of goods containing steel. Products whose access to these markets is restricted are being redirected to other countries, increasing import pressure on the EU.
According to an estimate cited in the presentation, based on data from EUROMETAL and Metals Consulting International, some trade flows previously destined for the US and Canada—accounting for more than 15% of global trade in steel derivative products—have been redirected to the EU.
The presentation mentioned Section 232 measures and melt-and-pour requirements in the US market, as well as corresponding Canadian customs rules. The document noted that the EU’s lower trade barriers for goods containing steel increase the risk of trade diversion and dumping.
Carbon costs undermine export competitiveness
Julius said CBAM is becoming an additional cost for manufacturers that use steel: European companies have to factor carbon charges and higher raw material costs resulting from trade measures into their product prices.
According to him, it is difficult for these companies to compete in third-country markets where comparable costs do not apply. Julius stressed that the issue concerns not only imports into the EU but also Europe’s export opportunities.
According to the latest data available to EUROMETAL, no mechanism to compensate for carbon costs on exports is planned, Julius said. He added that EUROMETAL had proposed compensating for these costs along lines similar to the refund of value-added tax (VAT) on exports.
Criticism of the CBAM calculation methodology
The presentation also examined technical aspects of the financial phase of CBAM, which began on January 1, 2026. The section, prepared using data from Macrometal, analyzed weighted average emissions calculated based on current production methods, as well as benchmarks used to determine the equivalent of free allowances.
The presentation criticized increases in default emissions values for certain countries without clear justification. It also said some definitions of production methods do not accurately reflect actual production conditions.
Other issues raised included an additional 10% uplift to values for certain countries in 2026 and uncertainty over emissions monitoring methodologies.
EUROMETAL appeal backed by more than 500 organizations
Julius said EUROMETAL issued an appeal in April to protect the steel production chain. The initiative was backed by more than 500 companies, national federations and industry organizations.
According to him, the aim of the initiative is to inform decision-makers in Brussels and at the national level about the pressure caused by imports of goods containing steel. Julius added that, at the request of policymakers, EUROMETAL is collecting data to demonstrate the growth in imports and their impact on production.
Julius highlighted differences in the trends for imports of finished steel products and goods containing steel. Recently, EUROMETAL has recorded quarterly growth of around 3% in imports of the latter category, he said.
Turkey’s hot-rolled coil quota also discussed
In his remarks, Julius also addressed Turkish hot-rolled coil (HRC) exports to the EU and considered how the new quota system affects trade flows and importers’ costs.
According to the presentation, Turkey’s country-specific HRC quota was 161,000 tonnes in each of the third and fourth quarters of 2026. An additional quota pool of 121,000 tonnes was available in each of those periods for countries covered by free trade agreements.
In July and August, HRC imports from Turkey into the EU totaled 289,000 tonnes. According to the data presented, this was about 7,000 tonnes above the combined volume of the country-specific quota and the additional pool.
The presentation listed Turkey among the countries with access to the additional pool in the third quarter, and Turkey and India in the fourth quarter. Julius noted that uncertainty over quota availability affects importers’ decisions and competition between countries.
He also said that Turkey has expanded its production capacity and improved product quality in recent years, enabling it to serve industries such as automotive more extensively. This should be taken into account when assessing trade relations with Europe, he said.
Julius added that the ability to pass rising costs on to end consumers and the sustainability of current price levels remain important issues.

Speaking at the Berlin Global Dialogue on October 22, Goyal said the EU risked hurting its own industries by imposing additional trade restrictions and compliance requirements, including the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). He pointed out that higher costs for steel and other industrial materials could undermine Europe's economic interests.
Goyal described the EU's approach as counterproductive, warning that the cumulative burden of regulations could hurt European industries while creating non-tariff barriers for trading partners.
Also read | ArcelorMittal & SA's IDC close in on $610 m deal
The minister pointed to the implications for infrastructure development, saying higher costs for steel, aluminium and cement would affect projects ranging from ports and airports to highways, utilities and water pipelines. He said the impact would be compounded by CBAM and deforestation-related requirements.
He also cautioned that countries could respond to restrictions imposed on their businesses with regulations of their own, potentially hurting European companies. In his view, the resulting increase in costs could push up inflation and make it harder for European industries to compete internationally.
The minister cited Germany's automobile sector as an example, saying car sales in the country had declined by 15-20% over roughly the past decade. He warned that further cost increases could put more pressure on the industry's ability to compete.
Goyal said India was focusing on improving its competitiveness while building mutually beneficial trade relationships with partner countries. He described India's trade agreements as fair, equitable and balanced, adding that the country was developing complementary economic strengths with its partners.
Also read | Welspun Corp’s $350 million US bet rides rising oil, gas pipeline demand
He also pointed to Singapore as an example of a trading partner without CBAM and deforestation-related requirements.
India has repeatedly raised concerns about the European Union's regulatory framework. Under CBAM, Indian exports of steel, aluminium and cement to the EU could face tariffs of 20-35%.
The EU's anti-deforestation regulation (EUDR) imposes compliance requirements on products linked to deforestation. The rules affect sectors including rubber, creating additional obligations for producers and exporters seeking access to European markets.
Goyal also highlighted India's relatively small contribution to global carbon emissions, saying the country accounts for 3-3.5% of the total while supporting 17% of the world's population.

articles.title: Will France’s Debt Crisis Stop the ECB From Raising Interest Rates Again? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Will France’s Debt Crisis Stop the ECB From Raising Interest Rates Again?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank (ECB) faces a difficult balancing act as it prepares to announce its latest interest rate decision, with rising energy prices pushing inflation concerns higher while France’s worsening debt crisis threatens to tighten financial conditions across the euro zone.
The ECB is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged on Thursday. However, investors will be watching closely for signals about whether another increase remains likely before the end of the year, particularly at the bank’s December 17 meeting.
The central bank has already raised interest rates twice this year as energy prices surged amid the Iran war. Yet the financial pressures confronting the euro zone have become more complicated since its September decision, with higher government borrowing costs coinciding with mounting political and fiscal uncertainty in France.
The ECB could use these developments to temper market expectations of another rate increase. However, it may prefer to avoid an explicit signal that further tightening is off the table, allowing financial markets to maintain pressure on governments while policymakers assess how the situation develops.
Why France’s Debt Crisis Complicates ECB Policy
France has emerged as a major source of uncertainty for the euro zone’s financial outlook. High government deficits, a prolonged budget impasse, street protests and an increasingly divisive election campaign have weakened investor confidence in the country’s fiscal position.
Over the six weeks following the ECB’s September rate increase, the premium investors demanded to hold French 10-year government bonds rather than German equivalents nearly doubled.
That widening spread matters because France is one of the euro zone’s largest economies and an important participant in its sovereign debt markets. If investors become increasingly concerned about French public finances, borrowing costs could rise further and potentially affect other countries in the currency bloc.
The ECB must therefore distinguish between higher borrowing costs that help control inflation and financial stress that threatens economic activity or disrupts the transmission of monetary policy across member states.
Higher yields can serve the central bank’s objectives by discouraging borrowing and spending. But if the French debt crisis pushes financing costs excessively higher, the resulting tightening could weaken demand beyond what the ECB considers necessary.
This creates a dilemma: the same market pressures that help the ECB contain inflation could eventually become a source of financial instability.
Are Financial Conditions Tightening Too Quickly?
The ECB’s decision will depend partly on whether higher bond yields are translating into a broader tightening of financial conditions.
The evidence remains mixed. The ECB’s Macro Finance Financial Conditions Index tightened sharply in September, reaching its highest level of the year, before stabilising toward the end of the month.
Other indicators initially suggested that financial conditions eased in early October despite mounting concerns about France. A weaker euro and stronger equity markets partly offset the impact of higher sovereign borrowing costs.
However, the picture subsequently changed. Goldman Sachs’ financial conditions index began tightening again, with its latest weekly reading showing a substantially larger increase than the corresponding US index.
Bank lending data also point to mounting pressure. The ECB’s September lending survey showed a sharp decline in mortgage demand, alongside tighter lending terms and standards for businesses and consumers.
France recorded the steepest fall in mortgage demand, reflecting deteriorating consumer confidence amid political uncertainty. French consumer confidence fell to its lowest level in 13 years, according to the figures cited in the analysis.
These developments could give the ECB grounds to signal that another rate increase is not inevitable. If borrowing costs are already restricting credit and economic activity, additional tightening could risk doing more damage than policymakers intend.
However, financial conditions do not depend on bond yields alone. Currency movements, equity prices and credit availability can offset or reinforce one another, making it difficult to determine whether the overall effect is sufficiently restrictive to change the bank’s policy outlook.
Why the ECB May Avoid Reassuring Markets
Despite the arguments for a more cautious approach, the ECB may have little incentive to explicitly discourage expectations of another rate increase.
The situation in France could change substantially before the bank’s next meeting on December 17. Budget negotiations, political developments, energy prices and the consequences of the Iran war all remain uncertain.
The ECB has also been careful not to make France’s debt problems the centre of its public communications. Its position has largely been that French fiscal authorities must address the country’s budget difficulties rather than expect the central bank to resolve them.
President Christine Lagarde has advocated a more measured approach to further monetary tightening, pointing to the limited evidence so far of second-round effects from higher headline inflation. These effects occur when an initial price shock spreads into wages, inflation expectations and broader prices.
ECB chief economist Philip Lane has acknowledged that rising bond yields amount to a material tightening of financial conditions and are relevant to monetary policy decisions. His remarks, however, concerned broader developments in bond markets, including spillovers from corporate borrowing linked to the artificial intelligence investment boom.
The central bank may therefore prefer to keep its options open rather than send markets a clear signal that the tightening cycle is nearing its end.
There is also a political consideration. If French borrowing costs rise because investors are demanding greater fiscal discipline, some policymakers may regard that pressure as a useful incentive for the government in Paris to resolve its budget impasse.
An explicit promise of monetary support could weaken that incentive or create expectations that the ECB will intervene whenever sovereign borrowing costs become politically uncomfortable.
Could the ECB Intervene to Stabilise French Debt?
One potential safeguard is the ECB’s Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), an emergency bond-buying mechanism designed to address disorderly market dynamics that threaten the transmission of monetary policy across the euro zone.
The instrument could, in principle, help contain destabilising increases in sovereign borrowing costs. However, deploying it would involve difficult judgments about the source of market stress, the conditions for intervention and the consequences for fiscal incentives.
Deutsche Bank analysts have argued that the threshold for activating the TPI remains high and that Lagarde is likely to say as little as possible about France at the upcoming meeting.
At the same time, the analysts have stressed that raising interest rates to address inflation would not necessarily conflict with using the TPI to stabilise French debt markets.
The distinction is important. Interest rate policy addresses inflation across the euro zone, while an emergency intervention tool would seek to prevent dysfunctional market conditions in an individual member state from undermining monetary policy.
Nevertheless, even discussing extraordinary intervention could affect investor behaviour and political negotiations. The ECB must weigh the risk of allowing financial stress to spread against the possibility that intervention could reduce pressure on French authorities to address their fiscal problems.
What the Euro Is Signalling
Currency markets have already responded to changing expectations about the ECB’s future decisions. The euro has fallen by approximately 4.5% since the September rate increase, partly reflecting investor expectations that the French crisis could lower the eventual peak of the ECB’s tightening cycle.
A weaker euro can support economic activity by making European exports more competitive. However, it can also increase the cost of imported goods and energy, potentially adding to inflationary pressures.
This creates another complication for the ECB. If the currency weakens further because investors expect fewer rate increases, imported inflation could become more persistent, potentially strengthening the argument for maintaining a restrictive policy stance.
At the same time, a weaker euro can ease financial conditions by offsetting some of the pressure created by rising bond yields. That could reduce the immediate need for the central bank to respond to tighter credit markets.
The market reaction is therefore not a straightforward indication that the ECB should change course. Currency movements can simultaneously ease some financial pressures and intensify others.
What Happens Next?
The ECB’s immediate challenge is to preserve flexibility without encouraging investors to interpret caution as a commitment to lower rates or an end to further tightening.
The Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan are also expected to leave rates unchanged at their upcoming meetings, but their communications may be more consistent with market expectations of further increases by year-end. The ECB faces a more complicated combination of inflation pressures and sovereign debt concerns.
A cautious message from Lagarde could temper expectations of a December increase without ruling it out. Conversely, a firm emphasis on inflation risks could preserve the prospect of further tightening while leaving the French debt crisis to be addressed primarily through national fiscal policy.
Ultimately, the ECB must determine whether higher borrowing costs are helping contain inflation or beginning to threaten financial stability across the currency bloc.

articles.title: ECB holds rates, says it has tools to calm markets as French debt fears rise - Kuwait Times
articles.summary: ECB holds rates, says it has tools to calm markets as French debt fears rise  Kuwait Times
articles.full_text:
FRANKFURT: The European Central Bank said on Thursday it had crisis-fighting tools to deal with “disorderly” markets, seeking to ease concerns that France’s deteriorating public finances could shake the wider eurozone, as it kept interest rates on hold.
The meeting came hours after President Christine Lagarde announced she would step down in February 2027, ahead of the end of her term in October 2027. The ECB held its benchmark rate despite rising inflation driven by the energy shock from the Iran war, but opened the door to another hike in December.
At a press conference after the decision, attention turned to France, whose bond yields, which reflect government borrowing costs, have surged to their highest since 2002. Declining to comment directly on France, Lagarde said that “should market developments threaten the smooth transmission of our monetary policy, including through unwarranted and disorderly market movements, we have instruments available to respond”. But she appeared to play down the chance of imminent intervention, noting there were criteria for such a step. “Fiscal sustainability is a crucial anchor for broader economic stability,” she said.
France’s borrowing costs have risen sharply amid a standoff over a budget aimed at cutting the deficit and after protests, partly driven by demands for more public spending, turned into the worst street violence in years. There has been speculation that the ECB could use for the first time its Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), designed to counter disorderly moves in sovereign debt markets, but the criteria are strict and most observers believe France’s problems do not meet the threshold.
Lagarde’s early departure will allow European leaders to choose her successor before France’s presidential elections in the spring. She gave little away about her plans, saying only that she wanted to speak more freely on matters beyond monetary policy, which is likely to fuel speculation that the former French finance minister could campaign in the election, though she has previously ruled out running herself.
The decision to hold rates after two hikes earlier this year was widely expected. Eurozone inflation hit a three-year high of 3.8 percent in September, but the ECB said underlying inflation remained broadly stable. Lagarde said the governing council had “debated whether a hike was appropriate”, adding that “unless there were major developments, the direction of travel is quite clear”. — AFP

articles.title: ECB holds rates at 2.5% on the day Lagarde announces her early exit - Euronews.com
articles.summary: ECB holds rates at 2.5% on the day Lagarde announces her early exit  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, hours after President Christine Lagarde said she would leave next February, months before her term ends, as France's bond market turmoil and inflation at 3.8% cloud the outlook for the eurozone.
The European Central Bank (ECB) left its key deposit rate unchanged at 2.5% on Thursday, at a meeting overshadowed by President Christine Lagarde's announcement earlier in the day that she will leave her post next February, months before her term ends.
The pause comes as a sell-off in French government bonds pushes up borrowing costs across the eurozone, while inflation runs at 3.8%, almost double the ECB's 2% target.
The decision by the Governing Council, which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro, follows two rate hikes this year, the latest in September, as energy prices linked to the Iran war drove inflation higher. The rates on its main refinancing operations and marginal lending facility also stay at 2.65% and 2.90% respectively.
In its statement, the ECB said energy prices had "continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook".
Underlying inflation has "remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage", it said, but warned that the size and duration of the energy shock were "likely to drive up inflation and lower growth".
The central bank also acknowledged that financing conditions "have tightened since the Governing Council's last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth", and repeated that it was "not pre-committing to a particular rate path".
Inflation in the eurozone rose to 3.8% in September, up from 3.2% in August, and the pause had been widely expected.
Lagarde's departure
The meeting came just hours after Lagarde said she would step down on 7 February 2027, around nine months before her eight-year term ends.
The ECB gave no reason, but reports since February have linked the timing to France's presidential election in April 2027.
"I leave this institution with a sense of a good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," Lagarde said in a separate statement.
Her exit sets off a race to lead the central bank, with Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot seen as frontrunners.
Two other seats on the ECB's six-member Executive Board, including that of chief economist Philip Lane, also open up in the first half of next year.
France in focus
The decision lands in the middle of France's political and fiscal crisis.
French 10-year borrowing costs climbed above 5% last week for the first time since 2002. On Thursday, the yield stood at around 5%, with the gap over German debt at roughly 155 basis points.
Ratings agency Moody’s kept France’s Aa3 rating unchanged last Friday, but with a negative outlook, while a divided parliament struggles to pass next year's budget.
As Euronews reported ahead of the meeting, Dutch bank ING estimated that the rise in bond yields since September had done the work of a 25 basis point hike in Germany, and closer to 50 basis points in France.
"The bond market has taken over the ECB's job," it said in a note.
Lagarde has so far poured cold water on hopes of a rescue. Speaking in Bangkok earlier this month, she said that "the primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies."
In Thursday's statement, the ECB repeated its standard line that the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), its never-used tool to buy the bonds of countries facing unjustified spikes in borrowing costs, is "available to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that pose a serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy".
It also left its balance sheet policy untouched, with its bond portfolios still shrinking as it no longer reinvests maturing debt, even though ING had expected a quiet pause in that run-down.

articles.title: Financing Europe's defence build-up: National budgets and beyond - European Union Institute for Security Studies |
articles.summary: Financing Europe's defence build-up: National budgets and beyond  European Union Institute for Security Studies |

source_detail.name: European Union Institute for Security Studies |

articles.full_text:
Defence budgets across Europe are rising. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, combined with doubts over the future of US security guarantees, has prompted European governments to invest more in defence. According to EUISS calculations based on EDA and NATO data, spending by EU Member States was 56% higher in 2025 than it was in 2022, after accounting for inflation.
One challenge is sustaining and increasing this spending. Rebuilding Europe’s military capacity will require investment over many years. Yet many national budgets are under pressure from fiscal constraints, higher borrowing costs and competing domestic priorities.
Europeans also need to spend more cooperatively to reduce costs and secure economies of scale. The feasibility of cooperation is influenced by many factors, including national threat perceptions, operational cultures, defence planning cycles and national industrial interests, but well-designed financial incentives can make cooperation more attractive.
A second challenge is mobilising the investment needed for Europe’s broader defence ramp-up, including expanding defence production capacity, investing in R&D and making European infrastructure more resilient to possible sabotage or attack.
Europe’s defence financing instruments can all play a role in meeting these challenges. This landscape has grown increasingly complex. National budgets remain the main pillar of defence expenditure, but they now form part of a wider ecosystem of EU instruments, public financial institutions like the European Investment Bank (EIB) and private capital, whose role continues to expand.
This analysis maps the landscape of European defence financing and assesses the growing number of proposals to strengthen and expand this ecosystem, such as a potential new round of funding under the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument or multilateral borrowing mechanisms outside the EU framework. Ultimately, there is no silver bullet for Europe’s defence financing challenge. There is no alternative to sustained national spending, but it can and should be supplemented by additional sources of funding. While this will not remove the need for difficult fiscal choices, it will make higher defence spending easier and help drive Europe’s broader defence ramp-up.
The core: National spending
Beyond national budgets: Four priorities to sustain Europe’s defence surge
As defence expenditure has grown, so has the range of funding streams complementing national budgets. EU instruments, funding from public banks and private finance can all contribute to giving momentum and coherence to Europe’s defence ramp-up. The following sections set out four priorities for sustaining Europe’s defence surge:
- Fully exploiting the EU’s potential;
- Leveraging public financial institutions;
- Exploring joint borrowing beyond the EU;
- Mobilising private capital.
1. Fully exploiting the EU’s potential
The EU is the most important source of defence financing beyond national budgets, and it already has a range of instruments to support defence. These are mapped below. In essence, the EU can add value in three ways: by mobilising additional resources, by embedding defence priorities across the wider EU budget, and by using financial incentives to make cooperation more appealing for defence companies and Member States.
The EU is already contributing significant resources to European defence expenditure, both in terms of strengthening Europe’s defences and supporting Ukraine.
Beyond these defence-specific instruments, other EU instruments also indirectly contribute to providing additional resources.
Aside from providing additional resources for defence, EU instruments can also make cooperation more attractive, helping make European defence spending more efficient. For example, the EDF has contributed to the creation of partnerships between European defence companies that would probably not otherwise have worked together. On the demand side, EDIRPA, EDIP and SAFE have the same purpose.
There is a strong case for expanding EU defence funding, and using it more strategically by targeting funding at key capability priorities and at joint projects.
First, the EU can provide cheap financing to Member States with limited fiscal space. This is valuable in itself as it takes some pressure off national budgets and will allow Member States to increase and sustain defence spending. Additional EU financing could take the form of loans or grants. An extension of the Ukraine loan beyond 2027 in some form is likely to be necessary. In terms of funding Europe’s own defence, loan-based instruments may be more politically feasible, as responsibility for repayment rests with individual governments. A new round of funding under SAFE would be a powerful way to mobilise additional resources for Europe’s defence build-up.
The 2028–2034 EU budget could also be a sizeable source of defence funding. The Commission has proposed allocating €131 billion to defence, security and space, although this figure could be reduced. Much will also depend on how much of this envelope would go to defence specifically, and what funding logic it would follow. Looking beyond the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the idea of EU defence bonds remains a harder sell. Repayments fall on all Member States, and for many it is cheaper to raise and spend money nationally. Nevertheless, these concerns could potentially be overcome through mechanisms to tightly target spending at agreed priorities with clear added value for all Member States.
Second, EU funding can increase the efficiency of European defence spending by driving cooperation, reducing fragmentation and enabling projects that may otherwise not have been possible. Linking a new round of SAFE funding more closely to joint rather than national procurement would further strengthen incentives for cooperation. Beyond tightening eligibility criteria, additional inducements could include financing fewer projects at higher rates, and focusing funding on emerging areas where there are fewer established national industrial players. The key will be striking a balance between the eligibility criteria and the funding on offer. The structure of cooperation also matters. Forcing large groups of countries to cooperate is likely to backfire, as modest financing cannot substitute for political alignment, shared threat perceptions and common capability priorities. Financing aimed at fostering the emergence of groupings with a shared vision is more likely to lead to concrete joint projects.
Third, looking beyond the EU’s defence instruments to the Union’s broader toolkit and budget, the priority should be embedding defence considerations horizontally across EU instruments as much as possible. For example, any defence-related elements of a proposal should be taken into account as fully as possible when evaluating projects in areas such as innovation, regional policy, energy, digital connectivity or transport.
2. Leveraging the role of public financial institutions
Harnessing the role of public financial institutions should be a second priority. In recent years these institutions have played a growing role in funding defence, above all the European Investment Bank, but also other national promotional banks.
Fully harnessing the EIB’s potential should be a priority. There are obstacles to greater involvement of the Bank in purely defence-related projects, notably the higher level of risk associated with certain defence investments, which could jeopardise its AAA rating. Nevertheless, there is a strong case for the Bank to further expand defence lending. For example, the EIB could help de-risk investments in joint production by Ukrainian and European companies in the EU. More broadly, the EIB could take on a larger role in financing upgrades to critical infrastructure, including to support military mobility.
3. Exploring joint borrowing beyond the EU
There is growing discussion of borrowing mechanisms beyond the EU framework. One reason is that reaching agreement among a small group of countries could be easier than reaching agreement among all 27 Member States, and it could be easier to include non-EU partners such as the UK or Norway. Some options are already being explored. In March 2026, Finland, the Netherlands and the UK announced that they were exploring a new defence financing and procurement mechanism aimed at driving joint procurement(8).
The MDM and the DSRB pursue the same broad objective as EU instruments: mobilising additional resources for European defence and making cooperative projects easier to finance. EU institutions could be associated with both mechanisms, helping to coordinate projects. The EU could also be a co-investor when this aligns with its own priorities. For example, EU grants could provide targeted top-ups, and Member States participating in MDM projects could combine these with SAFE-style loans, if projects meet EU eligibility criteria.
4. Mobilising private capital
The private sector is playing a growing role in supporting Europe’s defence ramp-up. Venture capital is a particularly important source of financing for emerging defence players. European defence start-ups are set to raise over €9 billion in 2026, four times as much as in 2025.
Data also suggests that the EU is attracting a larger share of defence venture capital funding, with the EU share across NATO, Canada, Australia and New Zealand rising from 13% in 2024 to 21% in 2026.
 
There are limits to what private capital can do. Private capital can provide additional resources and momentum for Europe’s defence ramp-up. It can help promising defence investments get off the ground by allowing innovative companies that struggle to access financing to secure the funding needed to develop prototypes and pay contractors along their supply chains. Private capital may also have a role in defence-relevant infrastructure, especially where projects generate long-term re

articles.title: Lagarde quits ECB nine months early as eurozone faces fresh interest rate pressure - Cyprus Mail
articles.summary: Lagarde quits ECB nine months early as eurozone faces fresh interest rate pressure  Cyprus Mail
articles.full_text:
Christine Lagarde is stepping down as president of the European Central Bank (ECB) nine months earlier than expected, bringing forward a leadership contest at a time when renewed inflationary pressures and rising borrowing costs are causing fresh concern for businesses and households across Cyprus and the eurozone.
The ECB confirmed on Thursday, October 29, that Lagarde will leave her post on February 7, 2027, rather than complete her eight-year term, which was due to expire at the end of October next year.
In a video statement published on the bank’s social media, Lagarde personally confirmed her departure, explaining that she had informed fellow policymakers and ECB staff of her decision.
Reflecting on her seven years in Frankfurt, she described her time at the institution as “a great pride and a huge privilege”, thanking those who had helped fulfil its mission in Europe.
That mission, she explained, was to “be a rock, be solid, deliver price stability, financial stability”, before adding that she would leave with “a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future.”
According to the official announcement, Lagarde also informed European Council president António Costa of her decision earlier on Thursday, with the ECB’s Governing Council thanking her for her service and giving her a lengthy standing ovation.
Her departure comes at a particularly difficult time for the European economy, with renewed inflationary pressures, higher energy costs and growing concerns over borrowing conditions putting the ECB’s interest-rate decisions back in the spotlight.
For Cyprus, those decisions directly affect mortgage repayments, business financing and deposit returns, making the choice of Lagarde’s successor particularly relevant to the island’s banking sector and wider economy.
The announcement also comes on the same day as the ECB’s latest monetary policy meeting, with policymakers expected to keep the deposit rate unchanged at 2.5 per cent, despite growing speculation that further increases could follow before the end of the year.
Rising oil prices, linked to the continuing Middle East conflict and disruptions to energy supplies, have complicated the inflation outlook, leaving the ECB balancing the need to control prices against the risk of putting further pressure on economic growth.
Lagarde, who took over from Mario Draghi in November 2019, has already overseen one of the most demanding periods in the bank’s history.
Her presidency began shortly before the Covid-19 pandemic and subsequently saw the eurozone confront the economic consequences of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, soaring inflation, the energy crisis and an aggressive series of interest-rate increases.
As the Financial Times reports, her seven years at the ECB have been dominated by exceptional economic and geopolitical crises, including the pandemic, war in Europe, a major inflation shock and trade tensions with the United States.
The newspaper also recalled that Lagarde, now 70, had previously admitted believing she would serve for five years rather than eight when she accepted the position following discussions with French president Emmanuel Macron.
Her early exit follows months of speculation about her future, with the World Economic Forum emerging as a possible next destination. According to the Financial Times, she has been in discussions about taking over as its chair, although no appointment has been confirmed.
Lagarde will become only the second ECB president to leave before completing a full term, following the bank’s first president, Wim Duisenberg, who departed after five years.
Attention is now turning to who will replace her, with former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot and former Bank of Spain governor Pablo Hernandez de Cos among the leading names being discussed.
The Financial Times reports that the Dutch government is backing Knot, while Spain supports Hernandez de Cos, who currently serves as general manager of the Bank for International Settlements.
Their potential appointments come at a time when the ECB is preparing for a broader change in its senior leadership.
Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel is leaving on January 3, 2027, a year before the end of her term, to take up a senior position at the International Monetary Fund, while ECB chief economist Philip Lane’s term expires in May.
The three departures mean European leaders will have to settle several important appointments within a relatively short period, raising questions about the future balance of views within the ECB’s six-member Executive Board.
The timing is politically significant, too. By leaving in February, Lagarde gives European leaders an opportunity to agree on a successor before France’s presidential election in spring 2027.
Costa has confirmed that the process of choosing a new president will begin immediately, with the European Council responsible for making the final appointment.
Under the EU’s appointment rules, any candidate must secure the support of at least 16 of the eurozone’s 21 member countries, representing no less than 65 per cent of the currency area’s population.
The process also involves consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB’s Governing Council before the European Council makes its decision.
Cyprus will have a say through its participation in the eurozone, while Central Bank of Cyprus (CBC) governor Christodoulos Patsalides sits on the ECB’s Governing Council, which is responsible for setting monetary policy across the currency bloc.
A change of president does not automatically mean a change in interest rates, since monetary policy decisions are taken collectively. Nevertheless, the next ECB chief will inherit an institution facing difficult choices over inflation, economic growth and the cost of credit, with the latest rise in energy prices making those decisions all the more complicated.

articles.title: Northumberland's new data centres must bring 'local benefits' - BBC
articles.summary: Northumberland's new data centres must bring 'local benefits'  BBCUK considers forcing data centres to invest locally to meet new AI ‘covenant’  Financial TimesUK's Healey offers faster grid access for key data centres in AI push  ReutersTech giants hit by clampdown on data centres  The TelegraphGovernment sets out ‘presumption of consent’ for proposed data centres in draft planning policy statement  Planning Resource
articles.full_text:
New data centres must bring 'local benefits'
- Published
Government plans to impose "strict tests" on data centres before they can be built have received a cautious welcome in an area which could soon be home to three such facilities.
During Wednesday's Budget speech, Chancellor John Healey said new centres would face requirements to "invest in local communities, create local jobs and protect local water supplies".
The Conservative leader of Northumberland County Council, which gave US firm QTS the go-ahead for a £10bn facility at Cambois and is considering two more applications, said the sector was "absolutely critical" for the economy.
Meanwhile, the local Labour MP welcomed Healey's pledge but warned the "devil is in the detail".
Last month, Blyth and Ashington MP Ian Lavery called on the prime minister to regulate data centre developments like those in his constituency, fearing they would take up "scarce industrial land that could be used for other industries that create far more local jobs".
On Wednesday, the chancellor told the House of Commons: "When the NHS uses AI to treat patients, we want that data here, when our armed forces use AI to keep us safe, we want that data here."
He said if companies invested locally, created jobs and protected resources, they "will get the grid connections they need and, where necessary, be allowed to build onsite generation while they wait".
Speaking to the Local Democracy Reporting Service afterwards, Lavery said: "We have to listen to the residents much more than we have been."
He said the chancellor's pledge "broadly speaking does address the issues" being raised, but he was "not sure it could cover the impact of having three or four data centres within two square miles".
Northumberland County Council leader Glen Sanderson said of the QTS plans: "If it is done right and carefully then data centre development is absolutely crucial for a new economy and a new generation of people."

articles.title: Mark Carney Sets Fresh Target for Canada-EU Partnership After Trump Threats - Newsweek
articles.summary: Mark Carney Sets Fresh Target for Canada-EU Partnership After Trump Threats  Newsweek
articles.full_text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has set a new timeline for an unprecedented partnership with the European Union, saying he expects negotiations to conclude in June as Canada seeks to reduce its reliance on the United States amid tensions with President Donald Trump.
Carney said Friday that Canadian Cabinet ministers and European commissioners would meet in March to advance negotiations before he attends European Council meetings in June, when he expects the talks to conclude.
The proposed relationship would stop short of Canada joining the EU but could make it the bloc's first "associate member," a designation that has no precedent in EU treaties and has faced resistance from some European governments.
Read More on News
"In parallel, we are working towards the deepest possible partnership, short of accession—with Canada becoming the European Union's first Associate Member," Carney told reporters Friday.
The fresh timeline emerged at the end of a two-day Canada-EU summit in Montreal, where Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa launched an "Alliance for the Future" aimed at expanding economic, technological and security cooperation.
The White House on Friday referred Newsweek to Trump's comments to reporters last month, in which he called the idea of Canada becoming an EU associate member "laughable" and threatened economic retaliation if he viewed the move as hostile.
"If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump said. "If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe."
Newsweek reached out to Carney’s office and the European Commission for comment on Friday.
Why Canada Is Moving Closer to the European Union
The proposed partnership is part of Carney's drive to make Canada less vulnerable to U.S. economic pressure after Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods and repeatedly raised the prospect of Canada becoming America's 51st state.
Relations deteriorated further this summer after U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down and the Trump administration imposed 50 percent tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian imports. Ottawa responded with retaliatory tariffs.
Carney said at the time that Canada had recognized "that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship."
The U.S. accounted for 71.7 percent of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025, down from 75.9 percent the year before, according to Statistics Canada, the country's national statistical agency.
Carney has made diversification a central part of his response to Trump, arguing that economic dependence can leave countries vulnerable to political pressure.
That strategy has already pushed Ottawa closer to European allies. Addressing the European Parliament in September, Carney warned that economic integration had become a form of leverage and argued that countries needed sufficient resilience to prevent others from controlling their markets or threatening their sovereignty.
What Mark Carney and the EU Agreed in Montreal
Friday's summit produced more than a timetable for future negotiations.
Canada and the EU announced progress on digital trade, European investment in Canadian critical minerals and artificial intelligence as part of their new Alliance for the Future.
The two sides concluded substantive negotiations on a digital trade agreement designed to make it easier for businesses to operate across the Atlantic. Canada and the European Investment Bank also concluded negotiations on an agreement intended to encourage European investment in Canada's critical-minerals sector.
Canada will participate in a European supercomputing initiative, while the two sides will explore linking their instant-payment systems.
They also agreed to study the feasibility of sending Canadian liquefied natural gas to Europe, explore new undersea cable connections and begin negotiations on expanding Canada's participation in Erasmus+, the European student-exchange program.
Cooperation is also set to expand in defense, cybersecurity, Arctic security, border security and efforts to counter foreign interference.
Costa described the arrangement as potentially the closest relationship the EU has established with a country outside the bloc.
"Canada is by far the most European of non-European countries," he said.
Von der Leyen said geographic location should not determine the depth of a country's relationship with Europe.
"It is not so important where the countries are on the map," she said. "What is important are the values that a country defends and where countries stand in international relations."
Canada's 'Associate Member' Plan Faces a Major Hurdle
Despite Carney's June target, a significant disagreement remains over what the new relationship will actually be called and how it would work.
The joint declaration issued Friday does not refer to Canada as an "associate member." Instead, Canada and the EU committed themselves to defining an "ever-closer association."
Reuters reported before the summit that Germany was among EU countries resisting the associate-member terminology because the concept has no existing legal status and its meaning has not been defined.
That makes Carney's comments Friday notable: he continued explicitly to embrace the associate-member goal even though the term did not survive negotiations over the summit declaration.
Von der Leyen has also continued to support the concept.
"We want Canada as close a partner as possible to the European Union," she said Friday. "We know that Canada cannot be a full-fledged member of the European Union, but to have a relationship as close as possible, this is our goal."
Carney had sought to play down the dispute over terminology earlier this week, saying: "The good news is it doesn't matter about specific names or nomenclature. What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians."
Donald Trump's Threats Loom Over Canada-EU Talks
The negotiations carry particular geopolitical significance because Trump's policies have helped drive both Canada and Europe to seek greater economic independence.
Trump has imposed sweeping tariffs on Canada during his second term, while Canada has retaliated against U.S. goods. He has also repeatedly spoken of Canada becoming the 51st state, rhetoric Carney has forcefully rejected.
The tensions come days before the U.S. midterm elections, with Trump's Canada tariffs emerging as an issue in closely watched Senate races in Michigan and Maine, where Republican candidates have pushed back against the policy.
Earlier this year, Carney said the old U.S.-Canada relationship was not coming back. Yet he has also argued that a stronger, more diversified Canada could ultimately make it a better American ally.
His message in Montreal focused again on sovereignty rather than a clean break with Washington.
“Above all, this is about sovereignty,” Carney said. “Our ability to live our lives as we wish.”

articles.title: Sanctions: the UK perspective - Global Investigations Review
articles.summary: Sanctions: the UK perspective  Global Investigations Review
articles.full_text:
Sanctions: the UK perspective
This is an Insight article, written by a selected contributor as part of GIR's co-published content. Learn more about Insight
1 Introduction
Sanctions are restrictive measures aimed at achieving foreign policy or national security objectives. With the creation of the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) in March 2016, and its sister agency the Office of Trade Sanctions Implementation (OTSI) in October 2024, sanctions enforcement is a growing area of economic crime enforcement in the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom implemented its autonomous sanctions regime following its exit from the European Union on 31 December 2020.
The United Kingdom currently implements and enforces sanctions imposed by the United Nations as well as its own autonomous domestic sanctions regime (which incorporates the sanctions originally imposed by the European Union that were retained in UK law after Brexit) against individuals, entities and jurisdictions. These include various restrictive measures, such as trade sanctions (eg, arms embargoes and restrictions on dual-use items), financial sanctions (eg, asset freezes and restrictions on a variety of financial markets and services) and immigration sanctions (eg, travel bans).
Although the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office has overall responsibility for UK government policy on international sanctions, trade sanctions are generally implemented and enforced by OTSI.[1] Financial sanctions are administered and enforced by OFSI (with support from the National Crime Agency (NCA)) and immigration sanctions by the Home Office.
In addition to civil enforcement, criminal prosecution of sanctions violations may be pursued by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC), the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) or the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) upon referral by OFSI or OTSI. Regulators, such as the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), also ensure that regulated firms have adequate systems and controls in place to enable them to meet their sanctions obligations.
In this chapter, we set out an overview of the UK sanctions framework and consider how investigations may arise and best practices when initiating or responding to investigations.
2 Overview of UK sanctions regime
2.1 Statutes and official guidance
The United Kingdom has historically followed the United Nations and the European Union in applying sanctions. EU sanctions are implemented through regulations with direct legal effect in Member States,[2] with individual Member States being responsible for enforcement of EU sanctions.[3] Post-Brexit, EU sanctions no longer apply in the United Kingdom, but EU sanctions have been implemented in national law through secondary legislation. Existing EU sanctions regimes are addressed under the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 (SAMLA), which provides the legal basis for the United Kingdom to impose, update and lift sanctions following Brexit. The United Kingdom also has its own terrorist sanctions regime, under which entities in the regulated sector are subject to the Anti-Terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001, the Counter-Terrorism Act 2008 and the Terrorist Asset-Freezing etc. Act 2010.
OFSI has issued guidance regarding its approach to financial sanctions under SAMLA,[4] an enforcement guide that summarises its approach to compliance and enforcement, including the imposition of penalties,[5] and, together with the NCA and working in conjunction with law enforcement and financial sector partners, has issued “red alert” notices that promote awareness and provide guidance on specific urgent issues.[6] Broadly, the guidance shows that OFSI has high expectations with regard to sanctions compliance. In particular, licensing grounds are interpreted narrowly, and it is clear that general and specific reporting obligations are a key aspect of the United Kingdom’s sanctions enforcement apparatus. When assessing sanctions violations, OFSI will treat each breach on its own merits based on a number of aggravating and mitigating factors, and will place substantial value on cooperation and timely voluntary disclosure.
2.2 Persons to whom sanctions apply
UK nationals and entities established under UK law, and their overseas branches, must comply with UK sanctions regardless of where they are located or where their activities take place. UK sanctions also apply to any individual or entity either located in, or that carries out activities within, the United Kingdom. OFSI provides a number of non-exhaustive examples of how a UK nexus might arise, including a UK company working overseas, transactions using clearing services in the United Kingdom, actions by a local subsidiary of a UK company or actions taking place overseas but directed from within the United Kingdom.[7]
Restrictive sanctions measures apply to named individuals, entities, groups, sectors and countries. OFSI maintains the UK Sanctions List,[8] which sets out individuals and entities subject to financial sanctions. OFSI considers that if a designated person owns more than 50% of, or otherwise controls, an entity (directly or indirectly),[9] financial sanctions will apply to that entity as well.
Historically, unlike the situation in the United States, the UK sanctions regime did not include secondary sanctions. However, in July 2024, the UK government expanded its powers of designation under the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (as amended),[10] to allow it to designate persons providing financial services or funds to persons who were involved in either obtaining a benefit from or supporting the Russian government, effectively creating secondary sanctions-adjacent powers. The UK government used this new power for the first time on 24 February 2025 to designate Keremet Bank, a Kyrgyzstani financial institution.[11]
Council Regulation (EC) No.2271/96, known as the Blocking Statute and enshrined into law in the United Kingdom,[12] prohibits UK residents and companies from complying with certain extraterritorial legislation, specifically in relation to US sanctions on Cuba and Iran, unless they are exceptionally authorised to do so by the Secretary of State. It also allows UK residents and companies to recover damages arising from such legislation from the persons or entities causing them and prevents any foreign court rulings based on the blocked legislation from having effect in the United Kingdom.[13]
2.3 Exemptions and licensing
The UK sanctions regime provides for certain exclusions from the restrictive measures imposed under sanctions legislation in the form of exceptions or licences. With respect to exceptions, in certain limited situations and subject to conditions as set out in the legislation, particular activities are automatically exempt, meaning that parties may engage in the activity without a licence or authorisation. Alternatively, for activities that would otherwise be prohibited, parties may rely on a general licence or apply for a specific licence.
OFSI oversees applications for licences in relation to financial sanctions, and OTSI oversees licences for trade sanctions and associated ancillary services. The UK Export Control Joint Unit (ECJU) continues to oversee licences for goods and services subject to both sanctions and strategic export controls, or goods subject to export controls only. OFSI, OTSI and the ECJU will only grant a licence where it falls within the specific grounds identified in the underlying legislation. Generally, these cover areas such as basic needs, legal fees and disbursements, fees or charges relating to frozen accounts and other economic resources, payment of court judgments or arbitration decisions against a designated person, satisfaction of prior contractual obligations, humanitarian assistance activity, diplomatic missions, other extraordinary expenses and, most recently, divestment.[14]
OFSI may also grant licences in accordance with the United Kingdom’s domestic terrorist sanctions regime (without the need for specific licensing grounds) and can issue licences that are either specific to individuals or generally applicable to all persons designated under particular domestic terrorist sanctions regimes.[15] General licences can be used without making an application, but each general licence will include requirements for prior notification of use, record-keeping and reporting.[16]
Where an individual or entity seeks to import or export goods restricted by sanctions, such as dual-use goods (items with both a military and civilian use), a licence may be required from the ECJU or OTSI alongside one from OFSI.
2.4 Key jurisdictions
A number of jurisdictions are sanctioned by the United Kingdom. Of these, three are particularly significant: Russia, Iran and North Korea.
2.4.1 Russia
The United Kingdom has retained numerous economic, trade and financial restrictive measures on Russia that were originally imposed by the European Union in response to the annexation of Crimea and Sevastopol, and actions that undermine or threaten the territorial sovereignty and independence of Ukraine, which were further expanded in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Alongside asset freezes and travel bans, it is also prohibited to:
- import or export arms and related material to or from Russia;
- sell, supply, transfer or export a wide range of goods and technology (eg, military, dual-use, luxury, critical-industry, quantum computing and advanced materials, energy-related or oil refining goods, or sectoral software and technology) for use in Russia or to “persons connected with Russia”,[17] or to provide technical and financial assistance or other services in connection with the export, sale or transfer of such goods and technology;
- deal in certain transferable securities or money market instruments issued by persons connected with Russia;
- provide loans or credit with a maturity exceeding 30 days to persons connected with Russia;

articles.title: Who Balances a Rearmed Germany When France Can’t? - Geopolitical Monitor
articles.summary: Who Balances a Rearmed Germany When France Can’t?  Geopolitical Monitor
articles.full_text:
The unification of Germany without war gave credence to the power of dialogue over outdated methods such as military might. Realist predictions of a rearmed Germany made after the Cold War remained, for three decades, an illusion, further strengthening the idea of military power being a thing of the past. Inside the US cradle, Europe was dreaming of a different reality. Robert Kagan called this Europe’s “post-historical paradise of peace and relative prosperity.” Liana Fix’s Germany Rearmed: The Return of War and the End of Illusions fittingly ends its title with that phrase. But the illusion has only half ended, chiefly for Western Europe in relation to states outside it. Within its ranks, reality has yet to set in.
The Russian invasion of Ukraine pushed Chancellor Scholz to announce a special fund to raise German defence spending to 2% of GDP. However, it took the return of President Trump to make that commitment real. Two months after the inauguration, Chancellor Merz reformed the debt brake that prohibited an annual structural deficit above 0.35% of GDP. Defence spending doubled, and Germany is now pushing towards 3.5% of GDP.
Rearming from Weakness
But relative prosperity within EU ranks is also under pressure. Its economic hegemon is no longer rising. German industrial output today is roughly equivalent to its output in 2005. Production peaked in 2017 and has declined by an average of 2.3 index points a year post-Covid. The causes are structural, cumulative, and largely self-imposed: energy costs following the nuclear phase-out, two decades of regulatory burden, the disruption of Russian gas, and the transformation of China from a customer into a competitor. Even with strong industrial output growth in August, the automotive industry declined, reflecting its inability to compete with China. And while defence spending, along with the AI boom, is providing the manufacturing sector with the stimulus it needs, it is costing Germany the pan-European integration that Merz pursued.
In June 2026, Merz and President Macron agreed to scrap the €100 billion combat aircraft pillar of the Future Combat Air System, launched in 2017 to replace the Rafale and Eurofighter by 2040. In October, the joint Main Ground Combat System intended to replace the Leclerc and the Leopard 2 fell into confusion, with France’s top general stating that Germany had withdrawn from the project, and Berlin having to clarify that it was adjusting the cooperation programme while reiterating its commitment.
Germany has used the armaments exemption under Article 346(1)(b), which allows member states to bypass the EU single market rules for the production of arms, to focus its defence expenditure on domestic industry. While this exemption enabled France and Sweden to build their own defence sectors, Germany is using it at a time it also seeks to take the leadership role in Europe. A leadership role requires providing public goods. What Germany is building to provide is security, but the money may not be buying the right capability.
Germany’s 2026 military strategy concept, titled “Responsibility for Europe”, shifts from strategy to capability plan, setting markers for what it wishes to achieve – readiness by 2029; expanded capabilities by 2035; technological superiority by 2039. This situates Germany taking “responsibility for Europe” well past the European intelligence assessment of Russia being ready to attack a NATO country by 2030 or earlier. Or as the Kiel Institute has put it, the Zeitenwende has so far been a quantitative shock rather than a qualitative one.
Despite its industrial stagnation and military expenditure on conservative capabilities, Germany is becoming more powerful in Europe. And more importantly, its peer in the EU structure is declining.
Declining from Strength
France is not Greece, and to argue otherwise would undermine the strengths it retains. But it is sliding into the kind of fiscal position that once belonged to Greece and Italy. Without corrective action, its deficit is projected to reach 6.4% of GDP in 2027. The proposed budget targets bring the deficit down to 5%. However, Fitch puts the required deficit to stabilise the debt at 3%, the same figure as the EU threshold France has breached, placing it under the Excessive Deficit Procedure. Even full delivery of a politically difficult budget leaves the ratio climbing, because while France made a real consolidation in 2025 by cutting its primary deficit by 0.8 points of GDP, it has only returned the country close to where it stood in 2022, with more owed in interest. The consequence is that a third of French high-grade corporate bonds now price more cheaply than French sovereign debt, essentially investors are charging the state more than they charge the companies within it.
One reason for France’s fiscal complications is the common currency, which denies France the ability to devalue or print its way out of its conundrum. The other is credibility. Italy has a higher debt-to-GDP ratio, yet its spread over Bunds has widened less than France’s. This is largely due to the fiscal responsibility Italy has shown in the past decade, which includes improving its primary balance and transforming its financial institutions. France has not taken the same path, and the markets have noticed.
French politics offers no exit from this predicament. The minority government’s deficit-cutting budget may be passed through Article 49.3, essentially circumventing the parliament, but with the 2027 elections on the horizon, other parties are unlikely to compromise. Amongst the opposition, France’s leading politician is Marine Le Pen, who proposes a 60% ceiling on the debt-to-GDP ratio and a reduction of the deficit by 0.5% each year. However, this stands in stark contrast to other promises she has made, including lowering VAT on certain sectors and the retirement age, and the possible scrapping of income tax for those under 30 years old. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the left-wing pole of French politics, proposes cancelling the debt held by the central bank, essentially defaulting on its debt – a proposal far graver than the position France is in and one that would ruin foreign investor confidence for decades. This leaves France with some of the highest taxes in Western Europe and the lowest retirement age, and no governing coalition capable of reducing French expenditure.
The contrast with Germany is even starker. Berlin is borrowing heavily for infrastructure and defence, and Bunds regained their safe-haven status as investors rotate out of French paper. Germany has raised its 2026 and 2027 growth forecast from 0.5% to 1.3% and from 0.9% to 1.1% respectively, with debt-financed investment driving its recovery. The asymmetry is as much about credibility as it is about productive capacity. Germany is permitted to borrow more because it borrows from a stronger starting point and towards future capacity. France borrows to keep the existing machine running.
Too Important to Decay
The problem for Europe is that a strong France remains a central pillar of the continent. It is the second largest economy in the eurozone and the only European state with sovereign military design, production, and certification across every domain – nuclear, aviation, naval, and land systems. It is also the only counterweight to Germany in the EU structure.
French decline is fiscal, not indicative of the quality of its production. German decline is industrial. But fiscal decline forecloses options faster, and it forecloses the military ones first. The EU’s National Escape Clause – one of the few fiscally lenient mechanisms that Germany agreed to, and only because it remains conditional – allows member states to add up to 1.5% of GDP in defence spending through 2028. France has not applied for it. The clause that requires the deviation to not endanger medium-term sustainability is ill-suited for a state already under the Excessive Deficit Procedure. This leaves France with the one industry where it leads Europe outright and ranks among the leaders globally, but in which it cannot do what the Germans are doing.
The question then is no longer the binary of whether France is too big to fail or too big to save. France is simply too important to be allowed to decay. The European Central Bank could in principle deploy the Transmission Protection Instrument to buy French bonds, but Christine Lagarde has played down the possibility. As Paul Krugman argues, during the euro crisis, southern European states could claim they deserved rescue because they were already undertaking painful austerity. France is moving in the opposite direction, which prevents it from making that claim, and any rescue would face opposition from creditor states.
But a continent facing the realities of providing its own security needs France’s leading sovereign capability. Traditionally a sovereigntist, the French offer to Europeanise its capabilities goes starkly against its historical record. But France also accepted the constraints of following a common currency because the state has remained pragmatic. A franc would have been weaker than the Deutschmark, making French exports more competitive than they are under the euro. It would have also retained the ability to simply print more currency to manage its debt to an extent. In both cases France acted in line with the strategy it has pursued since the 1950s, that of embedding Germany into European institutions so it would remain oriented towards Western Europe.
France could pursue such a strategy because the US guarantee held balance-of-power considerations in abeyance, and German and European interests largely converged. When they have diverged, Germany the multilateralist has a record of choosing business interests over normative commitments to Europe. It chose tolerance towards Russia after Georgia and after Crimea. More recently, it has cancelled pan-European defence programmes in favour of domestic defence

articles.title: Chancellor considers NATO bank to fill defence spending hole - DPA Magazine
articles.summary: Chancellor considers NATO bank to fill defence spending hole  DPA Magazine
articles.full_text:
In June, the Government announced an additional £15 billion for the Defence Investment Plan between 2026-27 and 2029-30. In the Autumn Budget, the Government confirmed the remaining £4.7bn hole would be filled by cutting capital budgets of all government departments by one per cent.
Now, Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is reportedly in talks about setting up an international bank to help increase defence funding to three per cent of GDP by 2030.
The proposed mechanism would involve the UK, Finland, the Netherlands and Poland. It could raise capital on international markets to finance defence purchases and provide funding for domestic defence companies.
Ministers are also expected to announce new requirements for overseas defence companies winning UK contracts to invest in the UK. The proposed rules would apply to contracts worth more than £50 million, with investment matching the value of the contract.
Tom Clarke, Partner in the Private Equity Group at global law firm White & Case, commented: “As governments across the world race to rearm, they are exploring a range of ways to fund defence.
“At the same time, there is a wall of private capital looking for opportunities in defence technology as previous investment restrictions are relaxed and investors rush to gain exposure to a highly attractive sector, with long-term structural growth tailwinds.
“Working with NATO allies could help the UK unlock further private capital and bring forward investment in new equipment.
“The UK is well placed to attract that investment, thanks to its mature VC ecosystem, deep pools of private capital and ready access to global money markets.
“The UK’s appeal as an investment hub is reflected in recent White & Case research, which found that 97 per cent of surveyed UK defence and defence technology companies regard the UK as Europe’s leading destination for defence technology investment.
“Governments are also seeking to build world-class sovereign defence technology capabilities to rebalance their reliance on other countries, and the reported plans to require overseas defence companies bidding for UK contracts to invest in the UK could further support this trend, strengthening domestic supply chains and defence capabilities.”

articles.title: European Commission grants €319m funding for next-generation semiconductors - Innovation News Network
articles.summary: European Commission grants €319m funding for next-generation semiconductors  Innovation News Network
articles.full_text:
€319m in Austrian state aid is being granted to Infineon Technologies to upgrade its semiconductor factory.
The factory is set to receive a €1.1bn upgrade, creating what it claims is the world’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for next-generation semiconductors.
These are gallium nitride (GaN) power semiconductors on 300mm wafers, something Infineon says it was the first company to achieve in 2024.
GaN semiconductors are becoming increasingly important
Since 2024, these semiconductors have been used more and more as they replace silicon in power electronics. They can handle higher voltages, switch faster, and operate at higher temperatures, all while using less energy.
Current uses include device chargers, AI data centres, electric vehicles, solar panels, wind turbines, 5G and 6G telecoms base stations, and robotics.
Their wafers are larger than the standard 200mm wafers, which allows for 2.3x more individual chips to be made per wafer and lowers manufacturing costs.
The European Commission will now fund Infineon to scale up production of these chips. In its announcement on 28 October, the measure falls under the EU’s Chips Act, and will “strengthen the EU’s position and autonomy in the semiconductor value chain.”
The Chips Act aims to boost the EU’s share of global semiconductor production from 10% in 2023 to 20% by 2030, while increasing domestic suppliers and demand for European-made chips.
Infineon, which currently holds a 29% market share in the power systems sector and 50% in the automotive chips sector, says this investment and factory upgrade in Villach will turn the facility into a “global competence centre for power semiconductors”.
“A strong commitment to Austria”
Christian Stocker, the Austrian chancellor, said: “This is not only a strong commitment to Austria as a business location but also helps ensure that the future of the semiconductor industry will not be shaped solely in Asia or the United States, but also in Austria and Europe.”
Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon Technologies AG, added: “This substantial investment shows our clear commitment to strengthening the European semiconductor ecosystem and Europe’s technological sovereignty. By establishing high-volume manufacturing on 300-millimetre wafers, we will be the first company in the world to bring gallium nitride power electronics into volume production.”
European policy is pushing to make more chips, including semiconductors, to reduce reliance on outside production and secure its business future. Dr. Luigi Capoani and Alberto Corso of the European Youth Think Tank wrote for INN about how the EU should approach this and what it needs to focus on to achieve the best results.
