articles.summary: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 29, 2026  Institute for the Study of WarPutin targets civilians in barbaric ‘safari’ attacks as Trump turns blind eye  The IndependentRussia unleashes killing spree against Ukrainian civilians on Thursday, targeting children, trains, and buses (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,708)  EUobserverRussia is intensifying daytime strikes on Ukraine and seeking to sideline Europe from peace talks – ISW  Mezha.netRuss...

source_detail.name: Institute for the Study of War

articles.full_text:
Toplines
Russian forces conducted devastating daytime long-range drone and loitering munition strikes against Ukraine on October 29, killing at least 19 and injuring at least 82. Ukrainian officials reported that a Russian jet-powered drone struck a commuter train at the Dnipro City railway station, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, killing at least 14 and injuring at least 14.[1] The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces launched four jet-powered drones against Dnipro City, and that Ukrainian forces intercepted three drones.[2] Ukrainian officials reported that Russian forces also conducted a Banderol loitering munition strike against a residential area in Chernihiv City, Chernihiv Oblast, killing at least two children and injuring at least 31 people, and a drone strike against an apartment building in Kremenchuk, Poltava Oblast, killing at least three and injuring at least 32, including six children.[3] The Ukrainian Air Force also reported that Russian forces launched 112 Shahed-type strike drones (40 of which were jet-powered) and Gerbera-type strike drones and Parodiya-type decoy drones against Ukraine overnight.[4]
The October 29 strikes are part of Russia’s continued effort to launch daytime strikes to make daily life in Ukraine untenable, inflict significant civilian casualties, and damage Ukraine’s economy. Russian forces have increased the brutality and lethality of their strike campaign throughout 2026, including conducting prolonged daytime and nighttime strike packages over several days designed to maximize civilian harm, leveraging vulnerabilities in Ukrainian air defenses, and introducing new technological adaptations like quasi-cruise missiles such as Banderols.[5] Russia’s October 29 long-range strikes, including against the Dnipro City railway station, demonstrate that Russia can inflict severe civilian harm when even a small percentage of drones penetrate Ukrainian defenses. Moscow is attempting to impose additional costs on the Ukrainian population ahead of Winter 2026-2027, as the Kremlin likely assesses that these long-range strikes can distract from Ukraine’s recent battlefield successes and ultimately force Ukraine into capitulation by making daily civilian life untenable.[6]
Russian President Vladimir Putin attempted to falsely portray Ukraine as the party responsible for the humanitarian catastrophe in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, where the limited ceasefire continues without reported violations. Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova reported on October 29 that there have been no ceasefire violations in Russian-occupied Oleshky for 54 hours since the beginning of the ceasefire on the morning of October 27.[7] Putin attempted on October 29 to falsely blame Ukraine for mining approaches to occupied Oleshky and creating a “humanitarian catastrophe.”[8] Russian occupation authorities, on the contrary, are fully responsible for the humanitarian crisis in occupied Oleshky, and Russian forces have been repeatedly and deliberately disrupting humanitarian aid deliveries and evacuation routes into the settlement.[9] Russian occupation officials also refused to abide by their obligations under international law to provide civilians in occupied areas with food and aid during conflict and have suspended food and medicine deliveries since May 2026.[10] The Kremlin’s repeated rejections of three Ukraine-proposed local humanitarian ceasefires forced Ukrainian forces to conduct a drone food delivery to Oleshky residents in September 2026, and Russian forces intentionally shot down the drones carrying these provisions.[11]
The Kremlin is attempting to drive a wedge between European countries in an attempt to undermine Europe’s negotiation position on the war in Ukraine and exclude European representatives from peace talks so long as they refuse to accept Russia’s demands, including NATO’s rollback to its 1997 borders.
Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov claimed on October 29 that Europe does not have a unified and consistent position regarding Russian President Vladimir Putin’s October 27 call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and noted that Russia did not expect this “inconsistency.
”[12] Ushakov also claimed that the current agreement involves only Ukraine-Russia-US trilateral talks, implying that European representatives will not be present at peace negotiations.
[13] Ushakov added, however, that Russia will have to negotiate with people whom Russia “does not really like,” when commenting on the possibility of future dialogue with Europe.
[14] Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov similarly claimed on October 28 that Russia must support European representatives who understand the need for a dialogue with the Kremlin in the context of peace negotiations.
[15] Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) Spokesperson Maria Zakharova claimed on October 28 that European leaders continue demonstrating their unwillingness to discuss “Russian interests” and are voicing “unrealistic demands on Moscow.
”[16] The October 28 and 29 Russian officials’ statements indicate that the Kremlin is attempting to deny Europeans a seat at the negotiating table until they accede to Russia’s December 2021 demand that NATO curtail its presence in Europe to its 1997 borders, effectively amounting to the destruction of the NATO alliance and requiring an overhaul of Europe’s security architecture.
[17] The Kremlin is also attempting to exploit Putin’s October 27 call with Stubb and Store to sow distrust among European states and thus weaken Europe’s negotiating position on the war in Ukraine.

The Kremlin is also likely setting conditions that would require Ukraine to make unilateral concessions before Russia agrees to engage in any meaningful peace negotiations in any format. Ushakov claimed on October 29 that trilateral negotiations between the United States, Ukraine, and Russia in Abu Dhabi will happen after November 4 (Russian National Unity Day) but noted that the date will depend on the “situation on the battlefield and the overall situation.”[18] Ushakov also noted that Russia will monitor whether Ukraine conducts large-scale strikes around Russia’s November 4 celebration, implying that Russia’s negotiating position will depend on Ukraine’s halting of long-range strikes despite the fact that the Kremlin has repeatedly refused to accept mutual long-range ceasefire agreements.[19] Kremlin officials have repeatedly weaponized exaggerated claims of Russian battlefield advances as leverage during peace negotiations to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine, often framing such concessions as prerequisites for any meaningful peace negotiations.[20] It remains unclear exactly what conditionality Ushakov’s October 29 statements refer to, but the Kremlin is likely setting conditions to establish arbitrary prerequisite demands that require unilateral Ukrainian concessions as conditions for renewing peace talks and frame Ukraine as the obstacle to peace if Ukraine fails to accept those demands.
Key Takeaways
- Russian forces conducted devastating daytime long-range drone and loitering munition strikes against Ukraine on October 29, killing at least 19 and injuring at least 82.
- The October 29 strikes are part of Russia’s continued effort to launch daytime strikes to make daily life in Ukraine untenable, inflict significant civilian casualties, and damage Ukraine’s economy.
- Russian President Vladimir Putin attempted to falsely portray Ukraine as the party responsible for the humanitarian catastrophe in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, where the limited ceasefire continues without reported violations.
- The Kremlin is attempting to drive a wedge between European countries in an attempt to undermine Europe’s negotiating position on the war in Ukraine and exclude European representatives from peace talks so long as they refuse to accept Russia’s demands, including NATO’s rollback to its 1997 borders.
- The Kremlin is also likely setting conditions that would require Ukraine to make unilateral concessions before Russia agrees to engage in any meaningful peace negotiations in any format.

We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.

articles.title: TUC leader expects wave of union recognition in private sector over coming year - The Guardian
articles.summary: TUC leader expects wave of union recognition in private sector over coming year  The Guardian‘Major Opportunity’ for UK Unions to Recruit Workers As New Rules Take Force  Novara MediaBusiness Exposed By Employment Rights Rush  Glasgow Chamber of CommerceUnions | Would you recognise a trade union access request?  HR GrapevineVideo: What to do when a trade union access request arrives  Personnel Today
articles.full_text:
The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, is predicting a wave of union recognition deals in the private sector over the next year as “transformative” rules on accessing workplaces come into force.
From Friday, as part of Labour’s Employment Rights Act, unions will have the right to enter workplaces or communicate with staff electronically. From January, employers will be obliged to inform workers of their right to join a union.
“I think it potentially could be transformative,” Nowak said. “This could open up large parts of … the private sector, where unions have been trying to get a foothold but have been hampered partly because of the legal framework. It gives us a real opportunity.”
He added: “My prediction would be that by this time next year, we’ll have signed hundreds, if not thousands of new recognition agreements with employers, taking that union voice into the private sector in particular.”
Polling carried out for the TUC by YouGov suggests 62% of workers would support a trade union negotiating on their behalf on pay and conditions, but 36% of those who are not members of a union say they would not know how to join one.
Nowak pointed to a flurry of recent deals, citing agreements between John Lewis and Usdaw and between the GMB and the Maritime and Coastguard Agency as evidence that some employers are responding even before the rules have come into force.
“What we’re seeing is a whole range of employers, who have recognised that the legislation is changing, that the political climate is changed and are now reaching voluntary agreements with unions,” he said.
Just over a fifth of the UK’s workforce are trade union members, down from more than half in 1979, before Margaret Thatcher came to power.
Under the new rules, there will be a formal process to request access to a workplace if a union cannot agree with the employer, which will be overseen by the regulator, the Central Arbitration Committee.
Previously, unions trying to win the right to represent a workforce have sometimes had to do so from outside the building – as was the case with the GMB’s thwarted effort to win recognition at Amazon’s warehouse near Coventry two years ago.
Nowak said Labour’s new approach “changes the mood, and I think it brings us much more into the European mainstream, which is that unions are part and parcel of the workplace”.
The access rights are the latest element of the government’s upgrade to workers’ rights to be implemented. Rights to sick pay have already been extended and further changes, including restrictions on zero hours contracts, are yet to come into force.
Some employers have complained about the potential costs of the new regime, but Nowak insisted good bosses need not worry.
“Genuinely, employers have got nothing to fear from this. They shouldn’t see their staff wanting an independent voice as somehow a negative verdict on them. You can work for a good, successful organisation and still want a strong, independent union voice.”

articles.title: Piyush Goyal’s Netherlands visit strengthens India-Netherlands Trade and Investment Partnership - India Shipping News
articles.summary: Piyush Goyal’s Netherlands visit strengthens India-Netherlands Trade and Investment Partnership  India Shipping News
articles.full_text:
ROTTERDAM: Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal concluded his two-day official visit to the Netherlands with a series of engagements on 25 and 26 October 2026, including a visit to the Port of Rotterdam, meetings with senior Dutch government leaders, parliamentarians and business leaders, and an interaction with the Indian diaspora.
The engagements focused on strengthening India-Netherlands economic cooperation and exploring new opportunities for trade and investment between Indian and Dutch enterprises. Minister Goyal was accompanied by a business delegation of approximately 60 people.
On 25 October, Shri Goyal began his visit with a tour of the Port of Rotterdam, accompanied by its Chief Executive Officer, Mr. Boudewijn Siemons. The visit highlighted the strategic importance of Europe’s largest port as a gateway for Indian goods to the European market and a key hub for global supply chains, and provided an opportunity to discuss strengthening collaboration between the Port of Rotterdam and Indian ports. The same day, the Minister met members of the Indian community at an event in Amsterdam organized by the Indian Embassy, and reaffirmed the diaspora’s important role in bilateral economic, cultural and people-to-people ties.
On 26 October, the Minister held bilateral meetings with Mr. Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, and Ms. Heleen Herbert, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy. The discussions covered expanded trade, resilient supply chains and greater Dutch investment in India’s manufacturing, R&D, infrastructure, renewable energy, logistics and digital technologies, as well as collaboration in semiconductors, green hydrogen, clean energy, critical minerals and advanced manufacturing, with a view to leveraging the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) to create new opportunities for bilateral trade and investment.
Shri Goyal also co-chaired the India-Netherlands Business Forum with Mr. Sjoerdsma, attended by approximately 200 representatives of Indian and Dutch businesses. Addressing the Forum, he said the elevated Strategic Partnership between India and the Netherlands offered immense opportunities that could contribute to a prosperous future for both countries. Following the Forum, the business delegation accompanying the Minister participated in sector-specific roundtables along with Dutch businesses covering High Technology and Innovation; Services and Allied Sectors; Agri-Food and Food Processing; Logistics and Supply Chain Connectivity; Sustainability and Renewable Energy; and Manufacturing, Pharmaceuticals, Textiles and Engineering Goods.
The Minister also held separate meetings with Mr. Arthur van Dijk, King’s Commissioner of the Province of Noord-Holland, and members of the Dutch House of Representatives Committee on Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation and the Senate Committee on European Affairs. He highlighted India’s rapid infrastructure development, its emergence as a global manufacturing hub and opportunities to deepen high-tech cooperation, and noted the potential of the FTA to benefit both economies.
Shri Goyal held individual meetings with CEOs and representatives of prominent Dutch companies, including ASML and Nexperia, leading players in the semiconductor sector; Power2X, developer of green hydrogen and renewable fuels projects; and Ingka Group (IKEA). The meetings explored opportunities for business partnerships and investment across sectors including semiconductor technology, electronics, logistics, energy and industrial solutions, technology and retail. He also participated in a Business Leaders’ Roundtable with CXOs of 15 Dutch companies, organised by the Embassy in The Hague in collaboration with HSBC Netherlands, where he shared India’s growth story and reform momentum and the opportunities for Dutch companies to invest, co-manufacture and co-innovate in India.
The visit built on the growing momentum in India-Netherlands bilateral cooperation and highlighted the potential of the trade and economic partnership, particularly in the context of the FTA and the Strategic Partnership announced during Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s visit to the Netherlands in May 2026.

articles.title: Duke Energy Selling Commercial Renewable Business to Brookfield for $2.8 Billion - Environmental Leader
articles.summary: Duke Energy Selling Commercial Renewable Business to Brookfield for $2.8 Billion  Environmental Leader
articles.full_text:
Duke Energy is selling its unregulated utility-scale commercial renewables business to Brookfield Renewable in a deal valued at nearly $2.8 billion.
The sale agreement includes more than 3.4 gigawatts of solar, wind, and battery storage capacity across the United States, joint venture partnerships, and current projects under construction. Duke Energy said it is in part selling the business to focus on the growth of its regulated businesses, including investments to enhance grid reliability and to help incorporate more than 30 GW of regulated renewable energy into its system by 2035.
Brookfield operates one of the largest publicly traded renewable power platforms, which includes hydroelectric, wind, solar, and battery storage facilities in North America, South Africa, Europe, and Asia. The company has nearly 31.6 GW of installed capacity and is developing some 132 GW more.
The deal will enhance Brookfield’s operations, the company said, by adding a proven renewable energy platform. It also strengthens the company as one of the largest renewable energy providers in the U.S., with almost 90 GW of operating and development assets, CEO Connor Teskey said.
Duke Energy said it expects to net approximately $1.1 billion from the sale, which is subject to adjustments. The primary operations of the commercial renewables business will remain in Charlotte, North Carolina, and current Duke employees working for the unit will transition to Brookfield to help maintain business continuity, the companies said.
Reuters reported that Duke Energy initiated the sale for the commercial renewables business in November 2022, and is planning to spend $65 billion over the next five years, most of that on clean energy transitions. Duke Energy, which owns more than 50 GW of energy capacity, has 8.2 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Ohio, and Kentucky.
"This sale is an important step in our transition into a purely regulated company with significant grid and clean energy investment plans that will deliver benefits to our customers and stakeholders,” Duke Energy President and CEO Lynn Good said.
The sale is expected to close by the end of 2023 and is subject to customary closing conditions including approval by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the expiration of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act. Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo Securities are serving as financial advisors to Duke Energy for the transaction, and Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom is serving as legal counsel, the company said.

articles.title: HMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist - The Guardian
articles.summary: HMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist  The GuardianPeter Hargreaves agrees to meet HMRC as it calls in billionaires  The TimesHMRC creates list of 200 billionaires in tax crackdown on UK’s wealthiest  Financial TimesHMRC draws up list of 200 billionaires in super-rich crackdown  The TelegraphHMRC targets 200 billionaires in crackdown on tax avoidance  The Independent
articles.full_text:
The UK’s tax authority is assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires as part of a crackdown meant to raise £500m for the public purse.
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) said it had for the first time compiled a list of billionaires who are required to pay tax in the UK, regardless of whether they formally live in the country, to tackle a “wealthy tax gap” caused by those who do not pay what they ought.
In an announcement after Wednesday’s budget, the authority said it was allocating a customer compliance manager (CCM) to each billionaire with a UK tax footprint, whose complex tax affairs are often hard for HMRC to manage.
“Billionaires can present a particular example of this, with affairs often spanning multiple taxes, entities and jurisdictions and a greater need for early and coordinated engagement,” HMRC said.
It said the managers would offer voluntary discussions to each billionaire before they filed their taxes, to “help build a shared understanding of the customers’ UK tax affairs and make subsequent engagement more focused and proportionate”.
The authority also plans to start deploying new tech to monitor wealthy individuals – defined as those with income of more than £200,000 or assets over £2m in any of the last three years – involving “advanced analytics, automated triggers and artificial intelligence (AI) to identify emerging risks earlier and target compliance activity where it will have greatest impact”.
It is part of wider efforts to tackle the wealthy tax gap, whereby rich people are failing to pay what they should if all of their assets were disclosed to the tax authority. The wealthy tax gap for 2024-25 was estimated to be worth £3.6bn, equivalent to 6% of the total tax gap across the UK’s entire tax-paying population.
The tax authority said its actions would contribute at least £500m towards a larger commitment to raise £10bn of additional tax revenues by 2030.
HMRC was grilled in July last year by MPs on the parliamentary public accounts committee over its lack of understanding of tax compliance by about 1.3 million wealthy taxpayers.
 
Adam Craggs, the head of tax, investigations and financial crime at the law firm RPC, said anyone with more than £200,000 of annual income, or net assets above £2m, should now “reflect on how clearly they understand and can evidence their UK tax position and their interaction with HMRC”.

articles.summary: ESO raises its 2026-2035 investment plan to EUR 4.4 billion to strengthen Lithuania's grid  energynews.pro
articles.full_text:
Energijos skirstymo operatorius (ESO), a subsidiary of Lithuanian group Ignitis grupė, is submitting its updated investment plan for 2026-2035 for public consultation. According to Ignitis grupė, planned investments rise from EUR 3.5 billion in the 2024-2033 plan to EUR 4.4 billion. The group attributes the increase mainly to additional spending on network resilience and the growing volume of new electricity customer connections.
Two strategic areas account for most of the spending
The first area covers network resilience and modernisation. It aims to ensure reliable electricity and gas distribution and faster restoration of supply after disruptions. In forested areas, ESO is replacing overhead lines with underground cables, with an overall target of placing 5,900 km of lines underground by 2030. By comparison, Enedis, the French distribution network operator, also publishes data on electricity usage.
The programme also includes renewing the ageing electricity network, maintaining the gas network, automating the electricity network, digitalising operations and installing smart meters. The planned budget reaches EUR 2.27 billion, or EUR 564 million more than in the previous plan.
Connections and renewable energy sources
The second area concerns new customers and renewable energy sources. ESO says it wants to connect new customers smoothly and integrate these sources optimally, making full use of existing infrastructure. The investments will fund new electricity customer connections, increases in permitted capacity, and the connection of prosumers and producers to the distribution network.
This programme has EUR 2.15 billion allocated, or EUR 354 million more than in the previous plan. ESO will finance the plan with its own and borrowed funds, European Union funding and other sources.
Timeline and approval conditions
The plan is updated every two years and submitted for agreement to the National Energy Regulatory Council (NERC), in accordance with applicable legislation. Specific investment projects will also be coordinated with NERC. The public consultation will last three weeks.
Ignitis grupė states that the amounts are planned investments and that publication of the plan does not constitute a final investment decision. Specific decisions, including scope, schedule and financing, will depend on regulatory approval, the availability of funding and other economic, legal and factual circumstances. If there are no material changes after agreement with NERC and approval of the final plan, no separate announcement will be published through the stock exchanges. The group adds that the information does not affect its Adjusted EBITDA and Investments guidance for 2026.

articles.title: Martin Lewis: 'How the new Starter Investment ISA could work – a possible boost to investing' - Money Saving Expert
articles.summary: Martin Lewis: 'How the new Starter Investment ISA could work – a possible boost to investing'  Money Saving Expert2027 ISA reforms scrapped – what you need to know  Hargreaves LansdownTurning Britain into a nation of investors shouldn’t be this complex  The TimesLet’s keep Isas simple  Financial TimesUK's Healey to reverse cuts to cash ISA allowances, FT reports  Reuters
articles.full_text:
In yesterday's Budget the Chancellor mentioned looking into setting up a Starter Investment ISA incentive. There's been some discussion about what it means...
We don't have much detail yet, but my suggestion was not for a new ISA. The ISA regime is already complicated. It was that first-time investors in a shares ISA should get a bonus on the money they put in.
This is something I first suggested to the former Chancellor Rachel Reeves (and repeated to the current Chancellor John Healey), when she was discussing reducing the cash ISA allowance "not to raise revenue but to get young people to invest". I thought it would be better to use a carrot rather than a stick.
As a totem, it would be a bonus of, say, 10% or 15% on the first £2,000 to £3,000 – though research needs doing on what the sweet spot is.
Some investment firms do offer intro bonuses at the moment, but it's patchy and marketing-driven. If you built it as a set allowance, people would understand it's constantly available, and it would be easier for someone like me to communicate without having to get involved in undue prominence for specific deals.
The concept is simple. Many people are risk averse and don't invest. But if you're putting money away for more than five years that you don't need in a broad spread of investments, it should hopefully substantially outperform savings.
The idea is to give nervous first-time investors an incentive to dip their toe in the water, knowing that because of the bonus - they've got wriggle room that if things did fall in the short term, they could still have more than they put in.
That was the concept. And that way, once they get used to it, some will be willing to continue and use the rest of their stocks and shares ISA, if they're lucky enough to have the money. Plus, if combined with an easy starter system that includes basic investment education, it could be a really powerful way to get more young people on the investment track.
I hope it comes to fruition and the investment sector adopts it. In many ways, what it's doing is standardising the minimum marketing incentive for a new first-timer, which firms occasionally offer anyway. As long as they're offering that minimum, they could say they're doing the official Starter Investment scheme. And if it's organised right, there's potential for it to be funded by the investment sector rather than by the state.
I hope you'll think it's worthy of the discussion.

articles.title: The European automotive industry's "protective shield" is still struggling against China's dominance. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The European automotive industry's "protective shield" is still struggling against China's dominance.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| “Made in Europe” – an initiative aimed at protecting the European automotive industry – has raised further serious concerns. (Image created by AI ) | 
 The EU's "Made in Europe" initiative is causing concern among global automotive component suppliers. Billions of dollars worth of trade and hundreds of thousands of jobs in Europe are at risk.
 Neighbors, but not close enough.
 The initiative, aimed at protecting the European automotive industry from allegedly unfair trade practices from China , the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), proposed in March, seeks to upgrade car manufacturing plants in the region and allocate subsidies specifically for vehicles produced in the region.
 However, the EU's plan to protect the "Made in Europe" automotive industry is causing deep concern among allied countries with automotive manufacturing sectors such as Turkey, Morocco, Japan, and South Korea , which are closely linked to the European supply chain.
 After months of deadlock regarding the potential impact of the IAA on their own countries' automotive manufacturing operations, Germany and France reached a crucial compromise earlier this month. Under this agreement, suppliers from non-EU countries, such as the United Kingdom and Norway, will also be recognized as meeting the “European origin” criteria.
 However, several other key partners in the European automotive industry will be excluded, including Türkiye, which has had favorable access to the EU market since the mid-1990s.
 Although these proposals still face numerous legal hurdles in Brussels before officially becoming law, Ayhan Zeytinoglu, President of the Economic Development Fund (IKV), believes that the Franco-German cooperation framework could have devastating consequences for the Turkish automotive industry.
 “73% of Türkiye’s total car exports go to the EU. Encountering a barrier called ‘Made in Europe’ would seriously damage Ankara’s trade and exports with its EU neighbors.” The expert also argued that, conversely, excluding Turkey could harm the European automotive industry itself, rather than enhance its competitiveness against overwhelming Chinese competition.
 According to calculations by the Turkish Automobile Exporters Association (OIB), Turkey's automobile exports to the EU totaled $30.1 billion (equivalent to €26.8 billion) last year.
 The IAA requires that 70% of the total value of vehicle components, excluding the battery, must be manufactured in Europe. However, the initial proposal only applied to battery-powered vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids, and fuel cell models, which last year accounted for only 27% of all new vehicle registrations in the EU.
 Tommaso Pardi, Director of the GERPISA international automotive research network and senior researcher at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), believes the 70% target is relatively achievable. Because if you exclude the battery from a typical European-made electric car, approximately 83% of the remaining parts are sourced from Europe.
 According to revised plans by Germany and France, some self-charging hybrid, petrol, and diesel vehicles could still be sold after 2035, while falling under the "Made in Europe" regulation. These models have a significantly lower percentage of European-made components. Therefore, if the regulation is applied with the proposed expanded scope, a large proportion of the nearly 800,000 Turkish vehicles exported to the EU last year would be affected.
 China seeks a "back door".
 Another important reason for Türkiye's exclusion is that Chinese automakers are expanding their presence in the economy hoping to gain a "backdoor" access to the EU market, but they have encountered significant obstacles.
 A typical example is SWM Motors, whose factory in Eskişehir (northwestern Türkiye) had to close after only one year of operation because the vehicles produced there did not meet EU safety standards.
 BYD's plans to build a $1 billion plant in Manisa, a major industrial hub near the Aegean coast, have also been put on hold.
 Meanwhile, according to consulting firm AlixPartners, since the Covid-19 pandemic, Morocco has attracted more than 10 billion euros (11 billion USD) in investment from China, largely concentrated in the production of batteries and automotive components.
 For France, Morocco plays a similar role to China for the German automotive industry – a low-cost production base that helps French car manufacturers maintain their competitiveness. Without Morocco in the production network, the cost of French models in the entry-level segment is likely to increase.
 Japanese automakers, many of whose models are assembled in factories in Europe, could also be at a disadvantage. Cars imported from Japan will not be eligible for EU subsidies; meanwhile, models manufactured in France, Portugal, or Eastern Europe will only receive preferential treatment if the percentage of components originating from Europe meets a specified level.
 South Korean automakers are also at risk. Hyundai and Kia currently assemble vehicles in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, but they also ship some models from Asia. These models would certainly not meet the standards for subsidies. However, South Korean battery manufacturing plants located in Poland and Hungary would still be counted as European production facilities.
 The difficult problem of "balancing under pressure"
 Beyond simply protecting the European automotive industry from Chinese competition, the EU must, more fundamentally, find a balance between industrial protectionism, competitiveness, and the interests of its partners in the global supply chain.
 Director Tommaso Pardi noted that European automotive giants are actively lobbying to loosen regulations in the IAA, with the goal of protecting their high profit margins. "They want to limit the scope of the IAA to retain as much of their ability to import components from abroad, especially from China," he said.
 EU automakers warn that rising component costs will put them at an even greater disadvantage against Chinese competitors, while European battery supplies are unlikely to meet demand in the near future.
 Ankara is also lobbying Brussels to be included in the “Make in Europe” program, while automakers are seeking a compromise that would allow Türkiye to participate in a later stage.
 According to expert Pardi, this solution “is only for European companies that have a presence there [in Türkiye and Morocco], and excludes all recent investments involving Chinese capital in these countries.”
 Meanwhile, European automotive parts suppliers hold the opposite view, calling for further strengthening of the IAA mechanism. They warn that without better protection for its members, the region could lose up to 650,000 automotive jobs by 2035.
 Benjamin Krieger, General Secretary of the European Automotive Parts Suppliers Association (CLEPA), warned, “Once jobs in the industry are lost, it is very difficult to restore them, and these losses will not be limited to large suppliers.”
 Mr. Krieger argued that the IAA helps European industry create a level playing field against unfair competition from China.
 Given the widespread public support for measures ensuring that EU public funding “benefits value creation in Europe,” Krieger from CLEPA believes that partners such as Turkey, Morocco, South Korea, and Japan could still benefit if they meet EU criteria.
 He stated that he welcomes partners who meet the criteria: "The EU should pave the way for parties to join the IAA through a voluntary mechanism based on objective criteria, including regulatory compatibility, social and environmental standards, non-distortion of the market, respect for the rule of law and the principle of reciprocity; all accompanied by anti-circumvention measures."
 Thus, the greater challenge in Europe's economic autonomy strategy is limiting the risk of China using third countries as springboards to access markets. However, distinguishing between investments that risk circumventing regulations and legitimate production activities by close partners is not simple. The line between protecting industry and erecting new trade barriers therefore becomes a key issue.

articles.title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia - The Guardian
articles.summary: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia  The GuardianG20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister  BBCG20 photocall cancelled after Ed Miliband and other foreign ministers refuse to be pictured with Russia's Sergei Lavrov  Sky NewsG20 foreign ministers skip photo-op amid objections over Russia  ReutersG20 photo scrapped amid tensions over Russian foreign minister’s presence&...
articles.full_text:
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

articles.title: 3 Killed as Ukraine Renews Drone Strikes Against Oil Refineries - The Moscow Times
articles.summary: 3 Killed as Ukraine Renews Drone Strikes Against Oil Refineries  The Moscow TimesUkraine Hits Russian Oil Refinery, Ending Pause and Defying Trump  WSJUkraine pauses strikes on Russian refineries after pressure from Trump, WSJ reports  ReutersAnother Russian refinery is aflame despite Trump’s warning to Kyiv  The Washington PostRussian oil refinery suffers major drone attack  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
At least two people died in the southern Samara region while responding to fires that broke out at industrial sites targeted in Ukrainian drone attacks overnight, local authorities said Friday, while a 19-year-old was killed in a separate airstrike in the western Bryansk region.
“During terrorist attacks on the civilian infrastructure of our region and country, the despicable enemy in Kyiv launched a record number of drones,” Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev wrote in a post on VKontakte.
He said emergency personnel were responding to damage caused by the airstrikes, as videos circulating on social media showed large plumes of black smoke rising from multiple buildings. Fedorishchev did not say which sites were struck.
The exiled news outlet Astra said it used those online videos to identify the targeted industrial facility in Samara as the Rosneft-owned Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery, which Ukraine has attacked multiple times in recent years.
Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed that Ukrainian drones targeted three oil refineries and one gas chemical complex overnight, saying at least one suffered “minor damage.” He did identify the facilities by name.
The attacks come after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine earlier this month, which neither side said they had agreed to beforehand. That apparent pause in strikes collapsed immediately as the Russian army continued its attacks against Ukraine's power grid.
The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Ukraine’s military had temporarily paused attacks on Russian oil refineries under pressure from the United States, where high domestic fuel costs are a major issue for voters ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly told journalists that “our guys tried to be a little more careful during these days,” but added that they were not explicitly told to avoid hitting Russian refineries.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 1,043 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Thursday night and Friday morning.

articles.title: Poland seeks stronger economic ties with India as EU trade deal advances - Times of Oman
articles.summary: Poland seeks stronger economic ties with India as EU trade deal advances  Times of Oman
articles.full_text:
Poland is seeking to strengthen its economic and strategic partnership with India following the conclusion of the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA), with Warsaw viewing the deal as an opportunity to expand trade, investment and cooperation across Central and Eastern Europe (CEE).
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk visited New Delhi on October 21, 2026, leading a delegation of nearly 100 companies. The visit was the first by a Polish prime minister to India since 2010 and followed the conclusion of negotiations on the EU-India trade agreement on January 27, 2026.
Negotiations for the agreement began in 2007 but stalled in 2013 before resuming in 2022. The deal connects two economic blocs accounting for approximately a quarter of global gross domestic product (GDP).
The European Commission expects EU exports of goods to India to double by 2032, with tariffs eliminated or reduced on 96.6 per cent of goods. The agreement also envisages improved access to India's services market and a quota-based system for automotive trade.
The agreement is expected to be signed in Brussels in December, with implementation targeted for early 2027, subject to the necessary approval, including consent from the European Parliament.
The agreement comes amid growing efforts by India and Europe to diversify supply chains and reduce strategic dependencies, particularly in response to tariff policies in the United States and export controls in China.
Polish-Indian trade stood at approximately $5.7 billion in 2024, making Poland India's largest trade and investment partner in Central and Eastern Europe. However, bilateral trade remains considerably smaller than India's trade with Germany and France.
Analysts note that tariff reductions alone will not guarantee an immediate increase in business. Their benefits will depend on companies establishing commercial relationships and developing investment partnerships.
Potential areas of cooperation include defence technology, military drones, electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum technologies, critical minerals and space. Polish electric bus manufacturer Solaris, through its joint venture with India's JBM Auto, offers an example of industrial cooperation.
During Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Warsaw in August 2024, the two countries established a strategic partnership and set a target of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.
Tusk has also promoted Poland as a gateway for Indian businesses seeking access to the wider European market. However, experts argue that Central and Eastern European countries could secure greater benefits by coordinating their engagement with India rather than competing individually.
The visit highlighted the potential for cooperation through the Visegrád group, comprising Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic. Discussions involving Indian and Visegrád foreign ministers could provide a framework for deeper regional engagement.
India's support for Poland's aspirations for a permanent place in the G20 was another significant aspect of the discussions, although the joint statement stopped short of guaranteeing membership. Poland, meanwhile, reiterated its support for India's bid for a permanent seat on an expanded United Nations Security Council.
Despite expanding economic ties, India's relationship with Russia remains a concern for Poland and other CEE countries, particularly in the context of the war in Ukraine.
The joint statement focused largely on the conflict's implications for food and energy security, while both sides emphasised the importance of a comprehensive and lasting peace consistent with the UN Charter.
The EU-India agreement is unlikely to transform Central and Eastern European economies immediately. Its long-term impact will depend on translating diplomatic engagement into commercial contracts, strengthening regional coordination and managing differences over Russia.
The agreement's anticipated signing and subsequent implementation in 2027 will provide an early indication of whether the region can turn the emerging partnership into tangible economic and strategic gains.

articles.title: UK’s Healey says government will fill defense plan gap by ‘reprioritizing’ - Defense News
articles.summary: UK’s Healey says government will fill defense plan gap by ‘reprioritizing’  Defense News
articles.full_text:
LONDON — Finance minister John Healey said on Wednesday “reprioritization” in other departments would fill a £4.7 billion ($6.3 billion) gap in Britain’s Defence Investment Plan, a blueprint government hopes shows its NATO commitment.
In his first budget, Healey said he would also adopt this approach of “looking hard at public spending” to set out the details of how Britain will meet the NATO commitment of spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035, and mark a target date for 3% in 2030.
“In today’s budget, I am fully funding the Defence Investment Plan, including through capital reprioritization across Whitehall. This honors the commitment made both by me – and by the prime minister,” he told parliament, referring to a part of London home to most government departments.
Healey, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Defense Minister Wes Streeting are under pressure to increase investment more quickly.
Confirming that detailed plans for reaching the 3% and 3.5% goals will be set out in a spending review planned next year, Healey said he was also “determined to use more innovative financing, alongside the private sector and our international allies.”
That delay in plotting a clear pathway to 3.5% will heighten calls by the main opposition Conservatives, who have demanded Healey’s resignation if he failed to set out a credible plan at the budget.
Healey resigned as defense minister under Keir Starmer in June over what Healey viewed as inadequate spending on defense, specifically over the former prime minister’s unwillingness or inability to find funds to reach the 3% goal by 2030.

articles.title: UK brings forward defense spending target, pledging billions to Ukraine - CNBC
articles.summary: UK brings forward defense spending target, pledging billions to Ukraine  CNBC
articles.full_text:
The U.K. has set out a target date for defense spending to rise to 3% of GDP, as the finance minister announced billions in aid for Ukraine in a “clear message to Moscow”.
John Healey on Wednesday set a target date of 2030 for the 3% figure, while reaffirming its NATO commitment to reach 3.5% by 2035.
Healey, who resigned as defense minister under the previous government over insufficient spending, presented his first annual budget as finance minister and highlighted a “new era of threat”.
“Today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes,” he said as he announced an additional £10 billion ($13.3 billion) in economic and military support, based on loans, export finance guarantees, as well as £500 million in urgent military funding for this winter.
The government will set out the details of how it will meet its defense spending targets at the spending review next year, Healey told lawmakers.
“As we look ahead to the spending review, we start from a position of strength, with spending at that higher base, there will be choices we have to make about priorities,” he said.
“Today, I’m getting work underway to get there in a fiscally sustainable way,” Healey said against the backdrop of strained public finances and increasing borrowing costs.
Healey also said the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will deploy up to £5 billion over the next four years into defence, dual-use technologies and other sectors supporting national security to strengthen the UK defense industrial base, support domestic supply chains and attract private investment.
Chris Beauchamp, chief UK market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, said Healey’s announcement lacked detail but “it looks like defence will get the money Healey said was needed when he was defence secretary.”
“The precise path will come through next year, but it seems like the spending bonanza for Rolls-Royce and others is still on the way. It just might take a little while to arrive,” he added.
Healey also announced that Rolls-Royce will develop its next-generation turbine engine technology in partnership with the U.K. government, in an investment worth £2.5 billion.

articles.title: ifo: Signs point to export growth - deutschland.de
articles.summary: ifo: Signs point to export growth  deutschland.de
articles.full_text:
According to the Munich-based ifo Institute, exports of many German industrial sectors are growing significantly. The automotive industry is among those driving the improvement.
Munich (dpa/d.de) – Export expectations in German industry have risen to their highest level since Russia launched its war of aggression against Ukraine. They climbed by 3.2 points to 12.2 points in October, according to the ifo Institute in Munich. “The automotive industry in particular has significantly revised its export outlook upwards,” said ifo Head of Surveys Klaus Wohlrabe.
In September, car manufacturers’ expectations were still clearly in negative territory at minus 15.1. They have now surged to plus 12.7. This means that the share of companies expecting rising exports is 12.7 percentage points higher than the share of those anticipating falling exports.
This isn’t the only good news: “The signs also point to export growth in many other industrial sectors,” says Wohlrabe. The export outlook is particularly positive in the beverage industry, among manufacturers of data processing equipment, electrical equipment, textiles and clothing, as well as in mechanical engineering.
Many German companies are also reporting encouraging quarterly figures. Mercedes-Benz’s third-quarter profits increased by around 28 percent, for example, while Deutsche Bank has continued its streak of record-breaking results with third-quarter profits in the billions.

articles.title: India-Netherlands Trade Push Gains Momentum - ET Edge Insights
articles.summary: India-Netherlands Trade Push Gains Momentum  ET Edge Insights
articles.full_text:
India and the Netherlands are looking to expand bilateral trade and investment, with Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal holding meetings with Dutch government leaders, parliamentarians and business executives to explore partnerships across semiconductors, clean energy, advanced manufacturing, and logistics.
Goyal concluded his two-day official visit to the Netherlands on October 25 and 26, accompanied by a business delegation of approximately 60 people. The engagements focused on expanding market access, strengthening supply chains and encouraging Dutch companies to invest, co-manufacture and co-innovate in India, according to a PIB release. The visit comes after India and the Netherlands elevated their bilateral relationship to a Strategic Partnership during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit in May 2026. The conclusion of the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) also featured in discussions on expanding trade and investment between the two countries.
Business Forum brings together 200 representatives
Goyal co-chaired the India-Netherlands Business Forum with Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Co-operation Sjoerd Sjoerdsma. The forum brought together approximately 200 representatives from Indian and Dutch businesses to discuss opportunities for commercial partnerships, investment and stronger supply-chain integration. The business forum was followed by sector-specific roundtables covering high technology and innovation, services, agri-food and food processing, logistics and supply-chain connectivity, sustainability and renewable energy, and manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, textiles and engineering goods.
The discussions were intended to identify opportunities for companies in both markets to work together, particularly in sectors where access to technology, manufacturing capabilities, and international supply chains could support cross-border business expansion. Goyal also met Dutch Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy Heleen Herbert to discuss trade, investment, and cooperation across manufacturing, research and development, infrastructure, renewable energy, logistics, and digital technologies.
Separate meetings were held with Arthur van Dijk, King’s Commissioner of the Province of Noord-Holland, as well as members of the Dutch House of Representatives Committee on Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation and the Senate Committee on European Affairs. During the visit, Goyal held individual meetings with representatives of semiconductor companies ASML and Nexperia, green hydrogen and renewable fuels developer Power2X, and Ingka Group, the parent company of IKEA. The discussions explored potential business partnerships and investments in semiconductor technology, electronics, energy, logistics, industrial solutions, and retail.
The meetings are particularly relevant to India’s efforts to expand manufacturing and strengthen its position in technology-intensive sectors. Engagement with semiconductor companies could open avenues for cooperation in advanced technology and electronics, while discussions with Power2X covered opportunities related to green hydrogen and renewable fuels.
Goyal also participated in a business leaders’ roundtable with senior executives from 15 Dutch companies. Organized by the Indian Embassy in The Hague in collaboration with HSBC Netherlands, the roundtable provided a platform to discuss investment opportunities, commercial partnerships, and the business environment in India. The minister invited Dutch companies to explore investment, co-manufacturing and innovation opportunities in India, according to the ministry.
Focus on Port of Rotterdam
Logistics and supply-chain connectivity were another focus of the visit. On October 25, Goyal toured the Port of Rotterdam, accompanied by its Chief Executive Officer, Boudewijn Siemons. The port is a major gateway for goods entering Europe and an important hub in international supply chains. The visit provided an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation between Rotterdam and Indian ports, with potential implications for cargo movement, logistics connectivity and trade infrastructure. For businesses trading between India and Europe, port connectivity, and efficient supply chains are important considerations alongside tariffs and market access. The discussions on port co-operation formed part of the broader engagement on strengthening the commercial links between the two countries.
Goyal also interacted with members of the Indian community in Amsterdam during the visit, according to the ministry.
India-EU FTA
The India-EU FTA was a key context for the minister’s discussions with Dutch officials and businesses. The agreement is expected to provide a framework for expanding commercial engagement between India and European markets, while the bilateral Strategic Partnership provides an additional channel for co-operation. The Netherlands’ role in European logistics, along with its companies’ capabilities in semiconductors, energy and advanced industrial technologies, creates opportunities for Indian businesses seeking technology partnerships and stronger international supply-chain connections.
The two-day visit concluded with discussions across government, industry, and logistics. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry said the engagements focused on identifying new opportunities for trade, investment, and collaboration between Indian and Dutch enterprises.

articles.title: Infineon to Build Europe’s First High-Volume 300mm GaN Power Semiconductor Manufacturing Facility - ELE Times
articles.summary: Infineon to Build Europe’s First High-Volume 300mm GaN Power Semiconductor Manufacturing Facility  ELE Times
articles.full_text:
Infineon Technologies AG is setting up Europe’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for gallium nitride (GaN) power semiconductors using 300-millimetre wafers. The company plans to invest around €1.1 billion in its existing cleanroom facilities at its Villach site in Austria by 2034, using and upgrading the current infrastructure to expand production capacity more efficiently and at a lower cost. Manufacturing is expected to begin by the end of 2027. The investment aims to meet growing demand for energy-efficient power chips used in AI data centres, energy infrastructure, electric vehicles, robotics and consumer electronics. GaN semiconductors can improve power-conversion efficiency, reduce energy losses and enable smaller, more compact electronic systems.
Infineon is a leading developer of gallium nitride (GaN) power semiconductors. Two years ago, the company achieved a major technological milestone by successfully processing GaN wafers measuring 300 millimetres in diameter. These larger wafers can produce around 2.3 times more chips per wafer than conventional 200-millimetre wafers, making manufacturing more efficient and cost-effective. Infineon is now moving this technology into high-volume production to supply customers with next-generation power semiconductors.
“This substantial investment shows our clear commitment to strengthening the European semiconductor ecosystem and Europe’s technological sovereignty. By establishing high-volume manufacturing on 300-millimeter wafers, we will be the first company in the world to bring gallium nitride power electronics into volume production,” says Jochen Hanebeck, CEO of Infineon Technologies AG. “In doing so, we are paving the way for the widespread use of gallium nitride in a wide range of key applications in areas such as artificial intelligence, energy infrastructure, e-mobility and robotics. This new, state-of-the-art manufacturing facility translates innovation leadership into direct customer benefits.”
Christian Stocker, Federal Chancellor of the Republic of Austria: “With Infineon’s billion-euro investment, we are witnessing one of the largest single investments in the history of Austria’s high-tech industry. This is not only a strong commitment to Austria as a business location but also helps ensure that the future of the semiconductor industry will not be shaped solely in Asia or the United States, but also in Austria and Europe. Villach will thus become home to a globally unique production facility for one of the key technologies that will shape the future. This will strengthen our international competitiveness and secure jobs and value creation in Austria. After all, Austria may not be a country with unlimited natural resources, but it is a country with an unlimited wealth of talent. Our cutting-edge research sets international standards, and companies such as Infineon demonstrate every day how innovation made in Austria works. These are precisely the strengths we want to build on with our industrial strategy so that, by 2035, Austria will once again rank among the world’s top ten industrial nations.”
Wolfgang Hattmannsdorfer, Austrian Federal Minister for Economic Affairs: “Chips are as important to tomorrow’s economy as oil was to yesterday’s. Europe currently accounts for only around 10 percent of global chip production. For me, the conclusion is clear: We must also manufacture this key technology in Europe. Austria is already a leader in energy-efficient chips. Relative to our population, we rank first in the EU in business R&D spending in the semiconductor sector. With our industrial strategy, we intend to build on this lead and not only research new technologies but also manufacture them on an industrial scale. This benefits the entire economy: Statistically, every job in the chip industry can provide six additional jobs across the broader economy. That is why we intend to support Infineon’s new chip production with up to 319 million euros – subject to clear funding criteria for the location. This will ensure that public funds strengthen value creation and jobs in Austria over the long term.”
The investment in this first-of-a-kind technology is being supported under the European Chips Act. The European Commission approved €319 million in state aid. The formal funding commitment by the Austrian Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs, Energy and Tourism is expected within the stipulated time limits. By approving the funding from the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs, Energy and Tourism, the European Commission is not only enabling the expansion of manufacturing capacities in Europe but is also generating positive spillover effects in related sectors – for example, through cross-border collaboration with universities and research institutions and improved access to innovative technologies and products for start-ups and small and medium-sized enterprises.
“Competitiveness and technological sovereignty emerge where excellent research is translated into industrial value creation. This is precisely where our flagship project comes in: From Austria, we are bringing innovation into industrial application, strengthening our technological leadership and securing highly skilled jobs. Microelectronics is a key industry with enormous leverage for the economy and society. The entire Austrian semiconductor ecosystem benefits – from research organizations and universities to industrial partners. We are thus sustainably strengthening Europe’s competitiveness and strategic autonomy in microelectronics,” emphasizes Sabine Herlitschka, CEO of Infineon Technologies Austria AG.
The investment strengthens Villach’s role as a global competence center for power electronics and new semiconductor materials. Infineon Austria currently employs around 5,800 people, approximately 4,800 of them at the Villach1 site. Together with universities, research institutions, start-ups and industry partners, Infineon forms the core of an internationally recognized microelectronics ecosystem in southern Austria. The establishment of the new 300-millimeter GaN manufacturing facility will also create positive synergies with the power electronics research and development activities located in Villach.
Gallium nitride is an advanced semiconductor material that can switch and convert electricity much more efficiently. This enables smaller, more powerful and more energy-efficient electronic systems with lower energy loss and reduced heat generation. Analysts expect the market for GaN power semiconductors to grow to approximately USD 3.5 billion by 2031, representing annual growth of around 35 percent between 2025 and 2031.2

On October 26, Goyal met with Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, and Heleen Herbert, Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy. Their talks addressed expanded trade, resilient supply chains, and increased Dutch investment in India’s manufacturing, research and development, infrastructure, renewable energy, logistics, and digital technologies. Areas for collaboration included semiconductors, green hydrogen, clean energy, critical minerals, and advanced manufacturing. These discussions were framed by the potential benefits of the India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) to increase bilateral trade and investment opportunities.
Goyal co-chaired the India-Netherlands Business Forum with Sjoerdsma, which was attended by approximately 200 business representatives from both countries. In his address, he stated, “The elevated Strategic Partnership between India and the Netherlands offered immense opportunities that could contribute to a prosperous future for both countries.” Following the forum, Goyal’s business delegation participated in sector-specific roundtables with Dutch companies across areas such as high technology and innovation; services and allied sectors; agri-food and food processing; logistics and supply chain connectivity; sustainability and renewable energy; and manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, textiles, and engineering goods.
The minister also held separate meetings with Arthur van Dijk, King’s Commissioner of the Province of Noord-Holland, and members of the Dutch House of Representatives Committee on Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, as well as the Senate Committee on European Affairs. Discussions focused on opportunities for partnerships and investments in semiconductor technology, electronics, logistics, energy and industrial solutions, technology, and retail.
Goyal also participated in a Business Leaders’ Roundtable with CXOs of 15 Dutch companies, organised by the Indian Embassy in The Hague in collaboration with HSBC Netherlands. During the event, he shared India’s growth story, reform momentum, and opportunities available for Dutch companies to invest, co-manufacture, and co-innovate in India.
This visit bolstered the growing momentum in bilateral cooperation and underscored the potential of the trade and economic partnership, particularly within the framework of the FTA and the Strategic Partnership announced during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to the Netherlands in May 2026.

articles.title: ‘Crazy’ Coalition making huge mistake by opposing EU trade deal: Turnbull - SMH.com.au
articles.summary: ‘Crazy’ Coalition making huge mistake by opposing EU trade deal: Turnbull  SMH.com.au
articles.full_text:
‘Crazy’ Coalition making huge mistake by opposing EU trade deal: Turnbull
New York: Former Liberal prime minister Malcolm Turnbull says the Coalition was “crazy” to oppose an EU free trade agreement and would be making a terrible mistake at a time when geopolitics compels Australia to build partnerships with countries other than the US.
Turnbull, who is sceptical that US leaders will return to multilateralism after Donald Trump’s presidency, said it was vital that Australia became more self-reliant in every respect.
“We should pursue our own self-interest as rigorously as Trump pursues America’s,” he said in an interview in New York.
“We’ve got to seek leverage where we can so that we’ve got more influence over global affairs. And we’ve got to build partnerships with other countries in our region and other like-minded nations.”
‘It’s in our interests to negotiate as many free trade deals as we can.’Former Australian prime minister Malcolm Turnbull
The Coalition is poised to vote down the European Union trade agreement in the Senate, led by opposition from the Nationals – although former minister Alex Hawke warned his Liberal colleagues it would be “nutty” to do so, as this masthead revealed on Thursday.
Turnbull said he was “really disappointed” in the Coalition – which he led twice – and that it would be making a “terrible mistake” by opposing the deal.
“Particularly given that that free trade agreement negotiation commenced under a Coalition government – that is to say, mine,” he said.
“Australia is a trading nation. We have low barriers to trade, low tariffs, and we have very few barriers to foreign investment. It’s in our interests to negotiate as many free trade deals as we can.”
At a separate function at the Australian consulate in Manhattan, Turnbull said the Coalition’s opposition to the deal would be “crazy”.
“But our politics has become crazier, like everywhere,” he said. “You can’t replace the United States, but those countries that still do believe in free trade should still nonetheless work together.”
One concern raised by members of both the Liberals and Nationals is that the proposed deal locks Australia into the Paris climate accord.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor called it a “dud deal” that would make net zero legally binding.
“The Europeans will be able to drag Australia through the courts because of a so-called free trade agreement,” Taylor said. “It’s not a free trade agreement – it’s a climate agreement.”
Turnbull, who ratified the Paris Agreement as prime minister, said Australia’s free trade deal with the United Kingdom featured the same language, which was ultimately “very weak” and akin to motherhood statements.
Opposing the trade deal would be “allowing culture war political considerations to get in the way of pursuing Australia’s economic interests”, he said.
Taylor’s office declined to comment on Turnbull’s remarks.
The government does not have a majority in the Senate but could still ratify the agreement with the support of the Greens. The party has not formalised its position, but leader David Shoebridge told Politico he was “looking at it with a favourable eye”.
At a news conference on Thursday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese adopted a similar position to Turnbull’s, noting that when he meets Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at international summits later this year, “Australia wants to be the country that [is] for free and fair trade unequivocally”.
‘A raging bull with a limp’
With Democrats likely to gain power in the US Congress at the next week’s midterm elections, and Trump serving out his second and final term, political attention is turning to what Trump’s final two years will look like, and the post-Trump world order.
Experts are divided on whether Trump – who will retain his executive power regardless of the midterm election results – will resemble a “lame duck” or a “raging bull” in his final two years.
“It’s probably a bit of both,” Turnbull said. “It’s probably a raging bull with a limp.”
But it was far from certain the US would snap back to its multilateral, free-trading instincts, he said.
Former president Joe Biden, a Democrat, kept many of the tariffs that Trump introduced in his first term, and the “America First” doctrine has broadened beyond Trump.
“I’m not confident that there’s going to be this flip back to previous values that were ones that we could share,” Turnbull said.
