articles.title: France, Mexico Align on Chronic Disease, Health Investment - Mexico Business News
articles.summary: France, Mexico Align on Chronic Disease, Health Investment  Mexico Business News
articles.full_text:
The opening of French Healthcare Day Mexico 2026 presented health as a strategic sector for investment between France and Mexico. Ambassador Delphine Borione said innovation must translate into a better patient journey. Patrick Devlyn of CCE outlined five opportunities in investment, clinical research, regulation, digital transformation, and patient outcomes. Javier Dávila Torres of the Ministry of Economy tied the agenda to Plan Mexico’s goal of growing the pharmaceutical industry three- to four-fold. ISEM’s Celina Castañeda de la Lanza stressed primary care and prevention as chronic diseases strain the system.
France and Mexico used the opening of the eighth French Healthcare Day Mexico to present health as a field for investment and industrial development, as well as a social priority. This year’s edition focuses on chronic diseases and emerging health challenges. Officials from both countries said the bilateral relationship, which marks its bicentennial in 2026, should now produce concrete projects in digital health, medical devices, biotechnology, and local production.
“Health should not be understood solely as a social priority or as a component of public spending. Health is also a strategic sector for Mexico and France,” says Patrick Devlyn, Head of Strategic Sectors, Business Coordinating Council (CCE), and CEO, Grupo Benedev. “It is a platform for innovation, investment, competitiveness, and economic development for both countries.”
Devlyn says France brings a long tradition of scientific excellence, biomedical research, and pharmaceutical innovation. Mexico, for its part, offers a large market, specialized talent, advanced manufacturing capabilities, and a platform for commercial integration with North America and, increasingly, with Europe. He outlined five opportunities the business sector should pursue. The first is attracting productive investment in pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, medical devices, and diagnostics. The second is strengthening clinical research and technology transfer so that Mexico becomes a regional reference center for research and development. The third is improving regulatory competitiveness through a COFEPRIS that is “increasingly competitive, modern, efficient, digital, and aligned with the best international practices.” The fourth is driving the digital transformation of the health system through artificial intelligence, telemedicine, and interoperability. The fifth, which he called the most important, is making sure this innovation translates into better outcomes for patients. “Investment requires legal certainty, clear rules, regulatory competitiveness, infrastructure, talent, and, above all, trust,” he says.
Delphine Borione, Ambassador of France to Mexico, says the event has become a fixed date on the bilateral health agenda. She notes that a declaration of intent signed last year by both countries’ health ministers set shared priorities. These include expanding access to care, improving the diagnosis and follow-up of chronic diseases, training health professionals, and putting women’s health at the center of the conversation. Existing cooperation already covers prevention, mental health, and research, and Borione says the goal now is to open new areas of work. “Innovation cannot be understood simply as a new technology. It must translate into a concrete improvement in the patient journey: earlier diagnoses, adequate treatments, better follow-up, accessible information, and closer care,” she says. She adds that digital health and electronic health records offer important prospects but require interoperability, data protection, and trust.
Javier Dávila Torres, General Director of Planning and Evaluation, Ministry of Economy, linked the agenda to Plan Mexico. He says that when the federal strategy was presented, the government set the goal of growing the pharmaceutical and medical device industry three- to four-fold during the current administration. A 90-day plan is now being developed with the pharmaceutical industry, he adds. He described Mexico’s past dependence on foreign suppliers during COVID-19, when the country realized it relied almost entirely on other nations for key inputs. He pointed to a technology transfer agreement with Sanofi that now allows vaccines to be produced in the State of Mexico. Dávila says Plan Mexico offers companies tax incentives, including deductions on asset purchases, but cautions that its success depends on continuity. “It is not an act of magic. It is an act of consistency, of confidence, of legal certainty, of protection of industrial property,” he says. He adds that the president’s personal involvement in COFEPRIS modernization is uncommon in his decades of public service. He also recalled that France’s SAMU emergency medical system was adapted in Mexico, as an example of how deep the cooperation already runs.
From the state level, Celina Castañeda de la Lanza, Ministry of Health of the State of Mexico and General Director, State of Mexico Health Institute (ISEM), described the burden that obesity, diabetes, and their complications, including chronic kidney disease, place on families and on the health system. Costly replacement therapies can push households into catastrophic spending, she says, so authorities are strengthening primary care infrastructure, where 80% of health conditions are treated, to start treatment earlier. She adds that the reemergence of measles is testing health systems once again. She says the State of Mexico and Mexico City share practically the entire metropolitan area, which puts additional pressure on services for the state’s 17 million residents.
Manola Zabalza Aldama, Secretary of Economic Development, Mexico City Government, framed the bilateral relationship through its scientific legacy. She cited pasteurization, which drastically reduced infant mortality, and work by Mexican scientist Francisco Bolívar Zapata on the pBR322 plasmid. Combined with French research on gene regulation, that work made it possible for bacteria to produce human insulin. “We are here to transform millions of lives through science and innovation, but also through the creation of dignified jobs,” she says.
The French delegation at this year’s edition includes companies specializing in surgery, regenerative medicine, diagnostics, nutrition, food supplements, and chronic disease care. Business France has positioned the French Healthcare Club in Mexico as one of its most active networks, and the agency’s recent work has extended to sports health and performance technology tied to the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The bicentennial has also driven joint initiatives between Business France and the French Embassy aimed at turning diplomatic momentum into business partnerships.

articles.title: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe - The Guardian
articles.summary: Perfume bottle and child’s necklace among treasures found in Pompeii wardrobe  The GuardianPompeii cupboard opens window onto life before Vesuvius erupted  ReutersIn Pompeii, a woman's wardrobe resurfaces with beauty items and jewels  Euronews.com'Thought to be lost forever': After 2,000 years, a library buried by Pompeii’s eruption is finally revealing its secrets  BBC Science Focus MagazinePompeii wardrobe found untouched since 79 CE holds a woman's keep...
articles.full_text:
Fragments of personal objects, from makeup tools and a perfume bottle to coins and a child’s necklace, have been found tucked away in a wooden wardrobe sealed off for almost 2,000 years in the ruins of Pompeii.
The artifacts provide an intimate glimpse of daily life in the ancient Roman city before it was devastated by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79. The wardrobe was discovered in a room of a home on Via dell’Abbondanza, which was one of the most bustling streets in Pompeii.
The items inside included tweezers, a small glass perfume bottle, an incense burner and a bronze lantern.
But the most intriguing relic was a necklace featuring more than 20 small charms crafted from various materials and representing several deities, including depictions of the gods Bes and Mercury.
The type of necklace, known as a crepundia, was traditionally worn by children. Its decorative charms rattled to help parents keep track of their children and could also help them be identified.
“A crepundia had a very special function,” said Gabriel Zuchtriegel, the director of Pompeii archaeological park.
“It was a reminder of their parents who perhaps lived far away … it was very typical of this society of people, who were often displaced. Many people moved around in the Mediterranean area and tended to carry personal objects with them.”
The wardrobe contained other items including 38 bronze coins, cooking pots and a wooden box with lead weights, suggesting that someone who lived in the home was a tradesperson.
The fact that money and personal objects were left behind could point to the owners having to flee the eruption at short notice, Zuchtriegel said.
Archaeologists also found the fragmented skeletons of two mice inside an amphora that had been kept in a storage area of the home.
The home had previously been associated with a person called Cornelius Maximus owing to the discovery of inscriptions, which are no longer visible. Its facade was first excavated in 1912, but experts are only now delving into some of its rooms as part of a wider restoration project.
There are also excavations under way at the Villa of the Mysteries in a suburb of Pompeii, which also first came to light in the early 20th century.
“It’s never been completely excavated, so we kind of want to finish the job,” said Zuchtriegel. “What’s interesting is that we’re not excavating in the part where the owners lived and where great frescoes are to be expected, but in the servants’ quarters.
“So what we hope to find there is more insight into the daily life and economy of those who were somehow in the shadow of history. The majority of the inhabitants in the Villa of the Mysteries were actually servants.”
Excavations at Pompeii regularly yield discoveries from the ruins of the ancient city. In 2025, a large and sophisticated thermal bath complex, which was thought to have been used by its owner to woo well-heeled guests, was found during excavations of a home on Via di Nola in Regio IX, a wealthy district of the city.
A home containing a cramped bakery, where enslaved people were believed to have been imprisoned and made to produce bread, was found in the same district in 2023.

articles.title: AstraZeneca launches $1.5B savings plan to fuel pipeline growth, says workforce won't shrink - Fierce Pharma
articles.summary: AstraZeneca launches $1.5B savings plan to fuel pipeline growth, says workforce won't shrink  Fierce PharmaAstraZeneca CEO strikes bullish tone on pipeline as stock rallies  ReutersAstraZeneca announces $2bn restructuring for drugs pipeline  The TimesAstraZeneca Launches $1.5 Billion Savings Plan to Fund Drug Pipeline  WSJAstraZeneca launches overhaul to cut costs by £1.1bn a year  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
Facing looming patent cliffs, AstraZeneca has launched a restructuring initiative aimed at generating $1.5 billion in annual savings by 2029.
Savings from the “Reshaping for Sustainable Growth” program will be reinvested “principally in the pipeline,” AZ said Friday in its third-quarter earnings announcement.
The company expects the three-year initiative to incur up to $2 billion in one-time restructuring costs.
The overhaul follows similar cost-cutting initiatives launched by Big Pharma peers, including Pfizer, Bristol Myers Squibb, Merck & Co., Novo Nordisk and GSK, in recent years.
AZ is refocusing its resources on pipeline growth following reports that a potential merger with BMS had fallen through. The reported combination, which would have created one of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies, faced investor pushback and raised questions about AZ's long-term growth outlook.
Following the merger speculation, AZ CEO Pascal Soriot told Bloomberg that the British pharma does not need a major acquisition to sustain growth beyond 2030.
During a press conference Friday, Soriot reaffirmed AZ's ambition to reach $80 billion in annual sales by 2030.
“We believe we have the science, the pipeline and the team to deliver,” he said.
While AZ is positioned to grow beyond 2030 without a major acquisition, Soriot said the company continues to look for opportunities to strengthen its portfolio.
“We are constantly looking at, how do we strengthen our presence in a franchise or another, in a disease or another, and how do we add more value to our portfolio in a company?” he said.
The restructuring is not expected to result in a net reduction in AZ's workforce, Chief Financial Officer Aradhana Sarin told reporters during the call. Although some positions will be eliminated, the company expects to create new roles as it reallocates resources.
“It won’t lead to a net reduction in jobs,” Sarin said. “We are a growing company. We still have big ambitions. I’d say net-net, we’ll still be adding jobs, maybe different types of jobs or jobs in different areas.”
“You don’t spend $1.5 billion without creating jobs,” Soriot said. “So right there, you see that there will be changes. It’s more reallocation of resources across the pipeline and across the world. In the end, we are still a growing company, and the idea is not to shrink the company. The opposite, actually.”
The executives did not specify which job functions would be affected, but Soriot said the restructuring would involve reallocating roles and resources across geographic regions and business functions.
Thanks to years of growth under Soriot's leadership, AZ was one of only three large pharmaceutical companies to consistently expand its workforce since 2021, a recent Fierce Pharma report shows. The company's last major restructuring initiative dates back to a separate $1.5 billion cost-cutting program launched in 2016, when its top-selling drug, Crestor, lost patent protection.
The latest restructuring comes as AZ, like its Big Pharma peers, faces several near- and mid-term patent cliffs. Its blockbuster SGLT2 inhibitor Farxiga is already competing with generics in the U.S. and China, with global third-quarter sales falling 25% year over year to approximately $1.6 billion.
Its antiplatelet drug Brilinta, PARP inhibitor Lynparza and respiratory medicine Symbicort have lost market exclusivity in certain markets. Meanwhile, the company faces additional patent expirations in the early 2030s for major oncology products, including the BTK inhibitor Calquence, EGFR-targeted lung cancer drug Tagrisso and PD-L1 inhibitor Imfinzi.
Against that backdrop, Soriot highlighted 23 key clinical readouts expected in 2027 that collectively represent more than $20 billion in potential peak annual sales. These include multiple phase 3 readouts for Daiichi Sankyo-partnered antibody-drug conjugate Datroway and the oral selective estrogen receptor degrader Etcamah in adjuvant breast cancer.
The two medicines are among 12 programs that Soriot said have non-risk-adjusted peak sales potential exceeding $5 billion.
On the dealmaking front, AZ recently completed a $2 billion equity investment in Summit Therapeutics as part of a broader collaboration focused on combining AZ's antibody-drug conjugates with Summit's Akeso-partnered PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody ivonescimab.
“The logic behind this partnership is maximizing the value of our ADC platform,” Soriot said. “And of course, the logic for Summit is to maximize the value of ivonescimab by combining it with ADC. That will be an important part of cancer care in the future.”
The Summit investment is one of several China-related deals struck by AZ, but potential regulatory changes in China and the U.S. could complicate future cross-border transactions.
China is proposing new rules that would block foreign acquisitions of certain advanced biotechnologies involving cell and gene therapies and small interfering RNA, or siRNA. Meanwhile, the U.S. Treasury Department has proposed expanding restrictions under the COINS Act to include certain pharmaceutical investments in China, which could prohibit some U.S. outbound investments in the country's biotech sector.
Soriot said AZ is closely monitoring the proposed regulatory changes and would comply with any new rules that take effect.
“But it’s important to remember that in science, collaboration is important, and in cancer or other diseases, people will want access to medicines that can save their lives,” he said.
If AZ licenses a product from China and commercializes and manufactures it in the U.S., Soriot said, the drug “becomes a U.S. product, saving U.S. lives.”

articles.title: Greenfield Global and European Energy Team Up to Produce 48,000 Tonnes of E-Methanol in Québec - energynews.pro
articles.summary: Greenfield Global and European Energy Team Up to Produce 48,000 Tonnes of E-Methanol in Québec  energynews.pro
articles.full_text:
A 48,000-tonne-per-year plant tied to a distillery
The planned facility would have an annual production capacity of 48,000 tonnes of e-methanol. It would combine renewable electricity with biogenic CO₂ from Greenfield Global's ethanol operations. According to the two companies, the distillery generates a high-quality stream of fermentation CO₂, which would give the project a contracted feedstock supply.
The partners say they chose Québec for its hydroelectricity, which they describe as among the lowest-cost and lowest-carbon-intensity in North America. They also cite existing industrial infrastructure, export routes to Europe and the domestic market, and a policy environment supportive of low-carbon industrial investment.
European, maritime and industrial outlets
The project aims to supply several markets, including those requesting European Renewable Fuel of Non-Biological Origin (RFNBO), maritime fuels and renewable polymers. The companies state that the e-methanol will meet RFNBO requirements.
Greenfield Global contributes the operating site, industrial infrastructure and biogenic CO₂. European Energy brings its experience in renewable energy and Power-to-X, a technology that converts electricity into fuels or chemicals. It operates the Kassø facility in Denmark, which the partners describe as the world's first large-scale commercial e-methanol facility, with an annual production capacity of 42,000 tonnes.
Talks with offtakers get under way
Preliminary engineering studies are complete and grid connection construction is underway, according to the two companies. They will begin commercial discussions with potential offtakers immediately. They have not yet specified the investment amount or the commissioning timeline.
Howard Field, Chief Executive Officer of Greenfield Global, says supply will follow demand for low-carbon fuels and chemicals only where projects are profitable. Knud Erik Andersen, Chief Executive Officer of European Energy, cites a desire to replicate the models that worked at Kassø. He presents Québec as a platform for future growth in North America.

articles.title: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe’s incumbency problem - Fortune
articles.summary: ‘It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is’: Octopus Energy CEO Greg Jackson on Europe’s incumbency problem  Fortune
articles.full_text:
The brutal business of selling mirrors is not for the fainthearted. The challenge is category differentiation, given that a mirror has one simple task—reflection. One of Greg Jackson’s first jobs was working for a mirror manufacturer which, at best, broke even or made a small profit. And then he had an idea.
“We started making mirrors that had really wide frames,” the founder of Octopus Energy (the U.K.’s largest energy provider) told me. “And on a picture [on the internet], suddenly we had a mirror that looked different from everybody else’s. And they sold like hotcakes—and that transformed the business.”
Approaching a business from a different point of view is an essential ingredient in the hunt for innovation. Jackson’s essential insight when it came to mirrors was that, online, every product looked the same. That is what the customer saw. And he realized that if the customer saw something different (a mirror with a wide frame), they might buy it. Which they did.
Not seeing something that is obvious to an outsider is a firm’s “incumbency cost”—embedded in the regular behavior of doing the same thing tomorrow as you did yesterday. It is one of the most significant brakes on the ability to grow.
“I think the single biggest factor affecting Europe—and an issue the U.S. is not immune to—is incumbency,” he told me. “China and the Gulf are not held back by incumbent industries. Instead they are, at huge pace, delivering the new world. If I look at electric vehicles as an example, there’s not an incumbent car industry in China that’s struggling to manage the transition to an entirely new technology. But if I look at Europe, European governments and consumers want electric vehicles, but the European car companies have not yet been able to be competitive at building them.”
Chinese electric vehicle sales in Europe are growing rapidly. Chery has tripled sales in Europe in the past year; BYD has doubled; Geely is up a third; and SAIC is up 23%. Taking the four leading Chinese carmakers together, their EV market share is now at 14.6%, up from 9.6%, according to the latest figures from the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association. In response to claims of state subsidized dumping by China, the European Union has applied duties of up to 35% on top of the standard 10% import tariff. Chinese cars are still over 20% cheaper to buy.
“Incumbents crowd out the innovators in many sectors and markets,” Jackson said. “It wasn’t the Post Office [the U.K.’s public mail service] that invented email. The music industry held back streaming and digital music for 10 to 20 years. What you need is routes to market for new technologies, and I think that can be a challenge in Europe because so many of the big industries essentially have a stranglehold on policy.
“Economists have said that nearly all productivity growth comes from new companies. If we want more growth, we need to allow creative destruction so new companies can deliver the productivity we need.”
Jackson said that Europe has a number of successful sectors that it can learn from. For example, the continent enjoys a vibrant and innovative fintech sector, whereas in America “they take my card around the back of the bar because their terminals and processes are so dated.” Few people have seen a check in Europe in more than a decade.
Octopus grew out of the need for a new way to manage energy supply and demand. Jackson initially attempted to convince legacy businesses that they would be far more efficient with a fully overhauled technology platform but, after not progressing very far, decided that he could build a team that could modernize more quickly.
“The idea was that through technology, we would be able to provide lower costs, because we’d be more operationally efficient,” he said. “We’d be more agile, so we can incorporate technologies like electric vehicles and solar panels and batteries directly into the energy system very efficiently. That would also help with cleaning up energy, because you can use more renewables more cost-effectively if you’re more agile. We set out building that company in 2015, and nine years later, we became the biggest energy company in the U.K., overtaking all the incumbents.
“We came from outside energy, we came from tech, and just like the people that built Uber didn’t come from personal transportation; and the people that built Airbnb didn’t come from hospitality; and the people that built Amazon didn’t own bookshops. What we were able to do is build an energy company not based around the assumptions of the industry, but using technology to meet the needs of customers.”
The brute force of market dynamics is pushing the world toward a different energy mix. In the European Union, wind and solar power produced more electricity than fossil fuels for the first time last year, according to Ember, the energy think tank.
“The technologies of electricity are improving exponentially, and the technologies of hydrocarbons are not,” Jackson said. “A car engine costs roughly the same now as it did 20 years ago. They’re not particularly more efficient. Meanwhile, an electric vehicle battery today costs 10 times less than it did 15 years ago. Solar panels cost 200 times less than they did 40 years ago. Wind turbines have come down two-thirds in price over the last 20 years.”
Jackson was in China earlier in the year and said that electrification is continuing at pace, with battery swap stations, rather than recharging, reducing the amount of time drivers have to wait to between three and five minutes. “It’s only when you see 49-ton trucks in China running on batteries that you realize how serious electrification is. The drivers don’t care about the price of diesel.” Which might give Donald Trump pause for thought as he eyes both the American midterm elections and the rising cost of fuel in the U.S.

                                        India's pharmaceutical exports grew nearly 5 per cent to $16.13 billion in the first half of the current fiscal year, driven by strong demand from Europe, ASEAN, and Latin America, according to Pharmexcil data released on Thursday.
Shipments stood at $15.38 billion in the same period last fiscal year.
According to data released by the Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India (Pharmexcil), the first-half performance saw growth across drug formulations and biologicals, bulk drugs and drug intermediates, and surgical products.
During the second quarter (July-September 2026), outbound shipments increased 3.05 per cent to $8.04 billion, compared with $7.8 billion in the same period the previous year. In the quarter, September recorded the highest monthly export value at $2,744.05 million, marking an increase of 4.68 per cent over September 2025.Region-wise, exports to Europe rose 9.66 per cent to $3,288.27 million, making up 20.38 per cent -- or over one-fifth -- of India's total pharmaceutical exports during H1 FY27.
Exports to the ASEAN region grew 21.54 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean rose 16.58 per cent, and shipments to Africa increased 6.48 per cent. These diversified geographic gains helped sustain overall export growth even as shipments to the US moderated during the period, Pharmexcil said.
Pharmexcil Chairman Namit Joshi said India has established its reputation globally on quality, affordable medicines, and large-scale manufacturing, and the next phase of growth must focus on moving up the value chain.
"The next phase of our growth should focus on moving up the value chain, where Indian companies are not just suppliers but active partners in pharmaceutical innovation," Joshi said, adding that Europe presents significant opportunities for co-development of complex generics, biosimilars, and specialised therapies.
Pharmexcil Vice Chairman Bhavin Mehta noted that double-digit growth in bulk drugs and intermediates reflects the breadth of domestic manufacturing capabilities.He added that continued investment in quality systems, advanced manufacturing, and regulatory preparedness will support greater global participation by Indian exporters, including MSMEs.
